The benefits allocation system provides positive outcomes at equal rates across protected demographic categories
The admissions algorithm produces acceptance decisions at statistically indistinguishable rates for applicants from different socioeconomic backgrounds

name: Adversarial Debiasing
description: Adversarial debiasing reduces bias by training models using a competitive adversarial setup, similar to Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The technique involves two neural networks: a predictor that learns to make accurate predictions on the main task, and an adversary (bias detector) that attempts to predict protected attributes (such as race, gender, or age) from the predictor's internal representations. Through adversarial training, the predictor learns to produce representations that retain predictive power for the main task whilst being uninformative about protected characteristics, thereby reducing discriminatory bias.

example_use_cases.description: Training a resume screening model for a technology company that evaluates candidates based on skills and experience whilst preventing the internal representations from encoding gender or ethnicity information, ensuring hiring decisions cannot be influenced by protected characteristics even indirectly through correlated features.

Developing a credit scoring model for loan approvals that accurately predicts default risk whilst ensuring the model's internal features cannot be used to infer applicants' race or age, thereby preventing discriminatory lending practices whilst maintaining predictive accuracy.

Creating a medical diagnosis model that makes accurate predictions about patient conditions whilst ensuring that the learned representations cannot reveal sensitive demographic information like gender or ethnicity, protecting patient privacy whilst maintaining clinical effectiveness.

limitations.description: Significantly more complex to implement than standard models, requiring expertise in adversarial training techniques and careful architecture design for both predictor and adversary networks.
Requires careful hyperparameter tuning to balance the competing objectives of task performance and bias mitigation, as overly strong adversarial training can harm predictive accuracy.

Effectiveness heavily depends on the quality and design of the adversary network - a weak adversary may fail to detect subtle biases, whilst an overly strong adversary may eliminate useful information.
Training can be unstable and may suffer from convergence issues common to adversarial training, requiring careful learning rate scheduling and regularisation techniques.
Provides no formal guarantees about bias elimination and may not prevent all forms of discrimination, particularly when protected attributes can be inferred from other available features.

sample_claims.text: The model's internal representations cannot be used to infer protected characteristics of individuals
The hiring system's learned features maintain predictive power for job suitability whilst being statistically independent of candidate gender
The credit scoring model's intermediate layers do not encode information about applicants' race or ethnicity
The diagnostic system achieves equitable performance across patient demographics without encoding sensitive attributes in its feature representations
The facial recognition model's hidden representations are uninformative about protected characteristics whilst preserving identification accuracy

name: Counterfactual Fairness Assessment
description: Counterfactual Fairness Assessment tests a model against the criterion of Kusner et al. (2017): a model is counterfactually fair if each individual's prediction would have had the same distribution had their protected attribute, such as race or sex, been different, with everything that attribute causes changed accordingly. The assessor first writes down a causal model, a graph of which variables cause which, covering the protected attribute, the model's inputs and unobserved background factors, and fits its equations to data. For each individual, the fitted model is used to infer the background factors from what was observed (abduction), set the protected attribute to another value (action) and recompute every input the attribute influences (prediction), giving a counterfactual version of that person. The model under test is run on the factual and counterfactual inputs, and the gap between the two predictions, per individual or as a distance between the two prediction distributions, is the evidence: distributions that lie on top of each other indicate counterfactual fairness under the assumed causal model. Every causal effect of the attribute counts as unfair, including effects that run through inputs it influences, such as test scores, which is what separates this criterion from versions that allow some pathways.

example_use_cases.description: A law school's admissions office uses a model to predict first-year grades from entrance-test scores and undergraduate grades. Its analysts build a causal model in which race and sex influence both inputs alongside an unobserved knowledge factor, fit it to past cohorts, and compare each applicant's predicted grade under actual and counterfactual race. A systematic shift shows that leaving race out of the inputs did not make the model counterfactually fair.

A credit risk team, working with economists, specifies a causal graph in which an applicant's ethnicity affects income and neighbourhood but not repayment behaviour directly, fits it to its applicant data, and checks whether the approval model's scores change for the counterfactual applicants. The result goes to the model risk committee together with the graph, because the conclusion holds only under that graph.

A public employment service reviewing a model that predicts job-seekers' risk of long-term unemployment from education and work history specifies, with labour-market researchers, how sex and migration background influence those inputs. It tests whether individual risk scores would change under counterfactual sex or migration background before the scores are used to allocate support.

limitations.description: The verdict rests on a causal model that cannot be checked against data: Kusner et al. note that counterfactual assumptions are generally unfalsifiable, even with experimental data, and should be treated as provisional. Different plausible graphs can give different verdicts, so a result is only as credible as the graph reported with it, and testing alternative graphs is part of the assessment.

A common cause left out of the graph, such as school quality affecting both test scores and later grades, biases the counterfactuals without any warning sign. Kilbertus et al. (2019) show that counterfactual fairness is sensitive to such unmeasured confounding and give tools to bound the effect for additive noise models, which adds a further analysis to do.

Every effect of the attribute counts as unfair, so a model that legitimately uses an input the attribute influences fails the test. Kusner et al. note that in practice few observed variables are unaffected by the attribute. Where some pathways are acceptable, for example where qualifications differ for reasons a decision may properly reflect, this criterion is stricter than the decision calls for.

Computing individual counterfactuals requires a fitted probabilistic model of the unobserved background factors; the original study fitted it in Stan, and DoWhy's counterfactual function needs mechanisms with additive noise and supports only continuous variables. With categorical inputs, many variables or unstructured data such as text and images, the assessment becomes hard to run or yields a spread of counterfactuals rather than one.

The counterfactual people are simulated by the fitted causal model, not observed. If its equations fit the data poorly or miss interactions, the counterfactual inputs are implausible and the measured gap reflects the causal model's errors as much as the predictor's; DoWhy's documentation notes counterfactual estimates are approximate for this reason.

sample_claims.text: Under the causal model agreed with the admissions committee, each applicant's predicted first-year grade has the same distribution under their actual and counterfactual race.
Under the documented causal graph linking ethnicity, income and neighbourhood, the credit model's approval scores do not change when applicants' ethnicity is counterfactually altered.

The unemployment-risk model's individual scores are unchanged under counterfactual sex and migration background, given the causal model reviewed by labour-market researchers, and the sensitivity of that result to unmeasured confounding has been bounded.

name: Causal Discrimination Testing
description: Causal discrimination testing checks whether a system gives different outputs to otherwise identical inputs because of a protected attribute, by changing only that attribute, or a name, term or other proxy that signals it, and measuring how often or how much the output changes. Galhotra, Brun and Meliou (2017), who called the approach fairness testing, generate inputs from a description of the valid input fields, make copies of each that differ only in the protected attribute (for example, recorded sex), run them all through the system as a black box, and report the causal discrimination score: the share of inputs whose decision changes, sampled until it is known within a chosen margin of error and confidence level. For text, the same test substitutes identity terms or names in otherwise unchanged sentences, such as one religion or ethnicity for another, and reports the average change in the model's score across the substitutions, which Garg et al. (2019) call the counterfactual token fairness gap. Because every other part of the input is held fixed, the test needs no model of how the attribute influences other variables: it measures whether the system itself responds to the attribute, or to the chosen proxy. The output is a score per attribute and, if the tester logs them, the input pairs whose outputs differed.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team tests a credit-approval model before release. For a sample of last year's applications it changes only the applicant's recorded sex, and separately their marital status, re-scores each pair, and reports the share of decisions that flip with a confidence interval, against a release threshold agreed with the compliance function.

A trust-and-safety team checks a toxicity classifier used to hold comments for review by substituting identity terms such as 'gay', 'Muslim' or 'Black' across a set of non-toxic comments. It measures the average change in toxicity score for each term and flags any term whose substitution pushes benign comments over the moderation threshold.

An HR technology supplier tests its CV-ranking service before a client deploys it, by submitting the same CVs under first names and surnames associated with different ethnicities and genders and reporting how often each candidate's rank or shortlisting changes.

A hospital's AI assurance lead tests a symptom-triage assistant with clinical vignettes that differ only in the patient's stated ethnicity. Clinicians first mark which vignettes should be unaffected by ethnicity, and only those pairs count as failures when the urgency rating changes.

limitations.description: Holding every other input fixed measures only the system's direct response to the attribute or proxy. It does not follow through the effects the attribute has on other inputs, such as career breaks on an employment history. Garg et al. note that token substitution is more limited than counterfactual fairness defined on a causal model. Where those downstream effects matter, a clean result does not show that individuals were treated fairly.

The test covers only what is perturbed. Unlisted identity terms, unperturbed proxies and multi-word references go undetected, as does discrimination that appears only when attributes change together: Galhotra et al. measured 11.2% for gender alone but 77.2% for gender, marital status and race together. Garg et al. found mitigation for listed terms generalised much less to held-out terms. A pass covers only the perturbations tried, and the list needs domain review.

Generated inputs may be unrealistic. Themis draws inputs uniformly from the input schema, so the score covers combinations that never occur in practice. Testing real inputs or an existing test suite avoids that, but the score is then only as representative as that set. Galhotra et al. note that Themis computes no confidence level for it, and an interval from a random sample of real cases covers sampling error only.

Not every substitution should leave the output unchanged. Garg et al. give 'That's so gay' versus 'That's so straight' as a pair a toxicity model may rightly score differently, and clinical risk can legitimately depend on sex. Without a judgement about which pairs must match, the test raises false alarms or, if such pairs are excluded wholesale, hides real failures.

A model can pass and still produce very different outcome or error rates across groups, because the test asks only whether changing the attribute changes the output, not whether outcomes are equal. Galhotra et al. distinguish this causal discrimination from group discrimination, and Garg et al. note that a text classifier can satisfy counterfactual fairness while completely failing equality of odds, so it does not replace group metrics.

sample_claims.text: Changing only an applicant's recorded sex changes the credit model's decision for fewer than 0.5% of last year's applications (upper limit of a 95% confidence interval from a random sample of them).
Substituting any listed identity term into non-toxic comments changes the moderation classifier's toxicity score by less than 0.05 on average.
Swapping names associated with different ethnicities and genders on otherwise identical CVs changes a CV's shortlisting outcome in fewer than 1% of the pairs tested.
The triage assistant's urgency rating changes in fewer than 1% of the vignette pairs that clinicians judged should be unaffected by the patient's stated ethnicity.

name: GAN-Based Tabular Synthetic Data
description: Generates synthetic tabular datasets using Generative Adversarial Networks, most commonly through architectures such as CTGAN (Conditional Tabular GAN) and TVAE (Triplet-based Variational Autoencoder). These models learn the joint distribution of mixed-type columns — continuous, discrete, and categorical — by training a generator and discriminator in an adversarial framework, with mode-specific normalisation to handle multimodal continuous distributions and training-by-sampling to address class imbalance. The resulting synthetic tables aim to preserve statistical relationships, correlations, and marginal distributions of the original data whilst containing no real records, supporting privacy-preserving data sharing, model development on sensitive datasets, and augmentation of limited training data.

example_use_cases.description: Generating synthetic patient records from hospital databases using CTGAN to enable multi-institution collaborative research on treatment outcomes without sharing identifiable health data across organisational boundaries.

Augmenting a limited fraud detection training set by generating synthetic fraudulent transaction records that preserve the statistical characteristics of rare fraud patterns, improving model recall on underrepresented fraud types.

Creating balanced synthetic datasets for credit scoring by generating additional records for underrepresented demographic groups, enabling fairness testing across protected characteristics without collecting new sensitive data.

limitations.description: Training instability inherent to GAN architectures (mode collapse, vanishing gradients) can result in synthetic data that fails to capture the full diversity of the original distribution, particularly for rare categories or tail distributions.
Requires substantial computational resources and hyperparameter tuning, with training times scaling poorly for datasets with many columns or complex inter-column dependencies.

Privacy guarantees are not inherent — without additional mechanisms like differential privacy, GAN-generated data may leak information about training records through memorisation or membership inference attacks.
Performance degrades significantly on datasets with high cardinality categorical columns, complex temporal dependencies, or relational structures across multiple tables.

sample_claims.text: The synthetic patient dataset generated by CTGAN preserves statistical correlations between clinical variables whilst containing no records traceable to real patients
The augmented training dataset includes GAN-generated records for underrepresented demographic groups, achieving balanced representation across all protected characteristics
The fraud detection model has been validated on GAN-generated synthetic transaction data that preserves the statistical distribution of rare fraud patterns from the original dataset

name: Statistical Oversampling Methods
description: A family of data augmentation techniques that generate synthetic minority-class examples through geometric interpolation in feature space, addressing class imbalance problems that degrade classifier performance on underrepresented groups. The foundational method, SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique), creates new instances by interpolating between existing minority samples and their k-nearest neighbours. Extensions include Borderline-SMOTE (focusing generation near decision boundaries), ADASYN (adaptively weighting harder-to-learn instances), and SVMSMOTE (using support vectors to guide generation). These methods operate directly on feature vectors without requiring neural network training, making them computationally lightweight and applicable to any tabular classification task.

example_use_cases.description: Applying SMOTE to oversample underrepresented ethnic groups in a loan approval training dataset, ensuring the classifier has sufficient examples from each demographic group to learn fair decision boundaries.
Using ADASYN to generate synthetic examples of rare manufacturing defect types, improving the reliability of quality control classifiers on edge cases that occur in fewer than 1% of production runs.

Applying Borderline-SMOTE to augment minority-class examples near the decision boundary in a medical diagnosis task, reducing false-negative rates for rare conditions without collecting additional patient data.

Oversampling underrepresented protected groups in a hiring dataset to enable equitable evaluation of candidates across gender and ethnicity, ensuring the model does not simply learn to predict the majority class.

limitations.description: Interpolation in feature space can generate synthetic instances that fall in regions of the feature space not occupied by the true data distribution, introducing noise or unrealistic combinations — particularly problematic for high-dimensional data.
Does not address the root cause of class imbalance (e.g. data collection bias, structural underrepresentation) and may mask rather than resolve underlying fairness issues in the data pipeline.
Performance degrades on high-dimensional datasets where the nearest-neighbour assumption breaks down, and oversampling in such spaces can amplify noise dimensions without improving classification.

Assumes the minority class forms coherent clusters in feature space; when minority examples are scattered or overlap heavily with majority-class regions, interpolation produces ambiguous or mislabelled synthetic samples.

sample_claims.text: The training dataset has been balanced using SMOTE oversampling to ensure the classifier has sufficient representation of all demographic groups for equitable decision-making
The rare defect classifier has been trained on an ADASYN-augmented dataset that maintains the original feature distributions whilst ensuring adequate representation of all defect categories

The diagnostic model performance on rare conditions has been improved through Borderline-SMOTE augmentation targeting samples near the decision boundary, without introducing fabricated clinical relationships

name: Sequential CART Synthesis
description: Sequential CART synthesis creates an artificial copy of a confidential microdata set (records about individual people or organisations) that can be released in place of the real data, in the form used by the synthpop package for R. Variables are synthesised one at a time in a chosen order: the first is generated by sampling with replacement from its observed values, and for each later variable a classification or regression tree (CART) is fitted on the real data to predict it from the variables earlier in the order. Each synthetic record is passed down that tree using its already-synthesised values, and the new value is copied from a randomly chosen real record in the leaf it reaches, so the joint distribution of the data is rebuilt as a chain of conditional distributions. Disclosure risk is limited by setting a minimum leaf size, smoothing synthesised continuous values and removing synthetic records that reproduce unique real ones, and several synthetic copies can be released so that analysts can allow for the extra uncertainty that synthesis adds.

example_use_cases.description: A national longitudinal study that links census returns to administrative records such as births, deaths and cancer registrations for a sample of the population cannot let approved researchers take the data off site. Its support team runs CART synthesis to produce a bespoke synthetic extract for each project, so researchers can explore the data and write and test their analysis code at their own institution before the final model is run on the real data in the secure setting.

A hospital trust wants a university team to develop a readmission model without receiving patient records. It releases a CART-synthesised copy of the admissions table with a minimum leaf size of ten and kernel smoothing of continuous values, removes any synthetic record that matches a unique real patient on age, sex and postcode district, and runs a disclosure-risk assessment before release.

A national statistics office publishes a synthetic teaching file of its labour force survey for university courses, generated by sequential CART synthesis with the variable order and minimum leaf sizes chosen with subject experts, and labels every record as synthetic so that no reader mistakes a row for a real respondent.

limitations.description: It gives no formal privacy guarantee. No synthetic record is a real person, but trees can reproduce rare combinations and extreme values, and an intruder who knows that a real record holds the largest value of a variable can bound it from the synthetic maximum. Risk must be measured for each release and reduced with larger leaves, smoothing and removal of unique matches, each of which costs analytical value.

Relationships the trees miss disappear from the synthetic data. A tree grown from few records may never split on a variable that matters, so the synthetic data show no association where the real data have one; in the method's original evaluation a regression coefficient for sex was attenuated to zero in this way. Small subgroups and weak effects are the most exposed.

Results depend on the order in which variables are synthesised and on which earlier variables predict each later one. A careless order can produce impossible combinations, such as a detailed category that contradicts the summary variable derived from it, so detailed variables should be synthesised before derived ones and the output checked for inconsistencies.

Synthetic data cannot reproduce every analysis of the real data. Analyses the synthesiser did not plan for may give different answers, so a release should state which analyses it supports, and users should confirm key findings on the real data, for example through a verification service or secure access.

sample_claims.text: The research extract released to the project team was generated by sequential CART synthesis with a minimum leaf size of ten and smoothing of continuous variables, and contains no record that reproduces a unique combination in the source data.

No confidential microdata left the secure environment during model development: external researchers wrote and tested their code on a synthetic extract, and only the final approved model was run on the real data.
A disclosure-risk assessment of the synthetic admissions table found no synthetic record matching a unique real patient on the agreed identifying variables.

name: Federated Learning
description: Federated learning enables collaborative model training across multiple distributed parties (devices, organisations, or data centres) without requiring centralised data sharing. Participants train models locally on their private datasets and only share model updates (gradients, weights, or aggregated statistics) with a central coordinator. This distributed approach serves multiple purposes: preserving data privacy and sovereignty, reducing communication costs, enabling learning from diverse data sources, improving model robustness through heterogeneous training, and facilitating compliance with data protection regulations whilst maintaining model performance comparable to centralised training.

example_use_cases.description: Developing a smartphone keyboard prediction model by learning from users' typing patterns without their text ever leaving their devices, enabling personalised predictions whilst maintaining complete data privacy.

Training a medical diagnosis model across multiple hospitals without sharing patient records, ensuring model robustness by learning from diverse patient populations and clinical practices across different institutions.

limitations.description: Communication overhead can be substantial, especially with frequent model updates and large models, potentially limiting scalability and increasing training time compared to centralised approaches.

Statistical heterogeneity across participants (non-IID data distributions) can lead to training instability, slower convergence, and reduced model performance compared to centralised training on pooled data.
System heterogeneity in computational capabilities, network connectivity, and availability of participating devices can create bottlenecks and introduce bias towards more capable participants.
Privacy vulnerabilities remain through gradient leakage attacks, model inversion, and membership inference attacks that can potentially reconstruct sensitive information from shared model updates.
Coordination complexity increases with the number of participants, requiring sophisticated aggregation protocols, fault tolerance mechanisms, and secure communication infrastructure.

sample_claims.text: The model training process does not require patient data to leave individual healthcare institutions
The diagnostic model performs reliably despite learning from patient populations with heterogeneous clinical characteristics across multiple sites
The keyboard prediction model learns from user typing patterns without transmitting personal text content to central servers

name: Differential Privacy
description: Differential privacy provides mathematically rigorous privacy protection by adding carefully calibrated random noise to data queries, statistical computations, or machine learning outputs. The technique works by ensuring that the presence or absence of any individual's data has minimal impact on the results - specifically, any query result should be nearly indistinguishable whether or not a particular person's data is included. This is achieved through controlled noise addition that scales with the query's sensitivity and a privacy budget (epsilon) that quantifies the privacy-utility trade-off. The smaller the epsilon, the more noise is added and the stronger the privacy guarantee, but at the cost of reduced accuracy.

example_use_cases.description: Protecting individual privacy in census data analysis by adding calibrated noise to demographic statistics, ensuring households cannot be re-identified whilst maintaining accurate population insights for policy planning.

Publishing differentially private aggregate statistics about model performance across different demographic groups, enabling transparent bias auditing without exposing sensitive individual prediction details or group membership.

limitations.description: Adding noise inherently reduces the accuracy and utility of results, with stronger privacy guarantees (smaller epsilon values) leading to more significant degradation in data quality.
Setting the privacy budget (epsilon) requires expertise and careful consideration of the privacy-utility trade-off, with no universal guidelines for appropriate values across different applications.
Sequential queries consume the privacy budget cumulatively, potentially requiring careful query planning and potentially prohibiting future analyses once the budget is exhausted.
Implementation complexity is high, requiring deep understanding of sensitivity analysis, noise mechanisms, and composition theorems to avoid inadvertent privacy violations.
May not protect against all privacy attacks, particularly sophisticated adversaries with auxiliary information or when combined with other data sources that could aid re-identification.

sample_claims.text: The census data analysis results remain statistically indistinguishable whether any single household's data is included or excluded
The medical research system's published statistics provide quantified privacy guarantees that bound the maximum disclosure risk for any individual patient
The model performance metrics across demographic groups are accompanied by documented privacy budget allocation and noise parameters
The system's privacy protection level is mathematically bounded and remains effective even under repeated queries within the allocated budget

name: Homomorphic Encryption
description: Homomorphic encryption allows computation on encrypted data without decrypting it first, producing encrypted results that, when decrypted, match the results of performing the same operations on the plaintext. This enables secure outsourced computation where sensitive data remains encrypted throughout processing. By allowing ML operations on encrypted data, it provides strong privacy guarantees for applications involving highly sensitive information.

example_use_cases.description: Enabling a cloud-based medical diagnosis service to process encrypted patient data and return encrypted results without the cloud provider ever accessing actual medical information, ensuring complete patient privacy during outsourced computation.

Protecting ML model intellectual property and confidential inference inputs during cloud deployment by running encrypted inference, ensuring that neither the client sensitive input data nor the server proprietary model weights and architecture are exposed to the cloud provider or the counterparty, enabling secure outsourced inference without requiring mutual trust assumptions.

limitations.description: Extremely computationally expensive, often 100-1000x slower than unencrypted computation, making it impractical for real-time applications or large-scale data processing.
Limited range of operations supported efficiently, with complex operations like divisions, comparisons, and non-polynomial functions being particularly challenging or impossible to implement.
Implementation requires deep cryptographic expertise to avoid security vulnerabilities, choose appropriate parameters, and optimise performance for specific use cases.
Memory and storage requirements are significantly higher than traditional computation, as encrypted data typically requires much more space than plaintext equivalents.
Current fully homomorphic encryption schemes have practical limitations on computation depth before noise accumulation requires expensive bootstrapping operations to refresh ciphertexts.

sample_claims.text: The cloud-based service processes patient data without the service provider ever accessing the underlying medical information
The financial analysis platform maintains data confidentiality throughout all computational operations performed by third-party infrastructure

name: Quantile Regression
description: Quantile regression estimates specific percentiles (quantiles) of the target variable rather than just predicting the average outcome. For example, instead of predicting 'average house price = £300,000', it can predict 'there's a 10% chance the price will be below £250,000, 50% chance below £300,000, and 90% chance below £380,000'. This technique reveals how input features affect different parts of the outcome distribution - perhaps property size strongly influences luxury homes (90th percentile) but barely affects budget properties (10th percentile). By capturing the full conditional distribution, quantile regression provides rich uncertainty information and enables robust prediction intervals.

example_use_cases.description: Predicting patient recovery times after surgery by estimating multiple quantiles (e.g., 25th, 50th, 75th percentiles), enabling doctors to communicate realistic timeframes: 'Most patients recover within 2-4 weeks, but some may take up to 8 weeks', providing robust uncertainty estimates for treatment planning.

Ensuring equitable loan amount predictions across demographic groups by verifying that the spread of predicted loan amounts (difference between 90th and 10th percentiles) is consistent across protected groups, preventing discriminatory practices in lending ranges.

limitations.description: Computationally intensive when fitting multiple quantiles simultaneously, especially for large datasets or complex models, as each quantile requires separate optimization.

May produce crossing quantiles without proper constraints, where predicted 90th percentile values are lower than 50th percentile values, creating logically inconsistent and unusable prediction intervals.
Sensitive to outliers and heavy-tailed distributions, particularly in extreme quantiles (e.g., 5th or 95th percentiles), which can lead to unstable and unreliable estimates.
Requires careful selection of quantile levels and may need domain expertise to interpret results meaningfully, as different quantiles may reveal conflicting patterns in feature relationships.
Less effective with small datasets where extreme quantiles cannot be reliably estimated due to insufficient data points in the tails of the distribution.

sample_claims.text: The flood forecasting model provides distinct uncertainty bounds for extreme and typical rainfall scenarios without assuming symmetric error distributions
The model's uncertainty estimates span consistently across protected groups when predicting both low-risk and high-risk outcomes
The patient recovery time predictions distinguish between typical cases and outlier cases without relying on normally distributed residuals

name: Conformal Prediction
description: Conformal prediction provides mathematically guaranteed uncertainty quantification by creating prediction sets that contain the true outcome with a specified probability (e.g., exactly 95% coverage). The technique works by measuring how 'strange' or 'nonconforming' new predictions are compared to calibration data - if a prediction seems unusual, it gets wider intervals. For example, in medical diagnosis, instead of saying 'likely cancer', it might say 'possible diagnoses: {cancer, benign tumour} with 95% confidence'. This distribution-free method works with any underlying model (neural networks, random forests, etc.) and requires no assumptions about data distribution, making it a robust framework for reliable uncertainty estimates in high-stakes applications.

example_use_cases.description: Creating prediction sets for drug discovery that guarantee 95% coverage, such as 'this compound will likely have activity against {target A, target B, target C}', ensuring reliable decision-making in costly experimental validation.

Providing transparent multi-class predictions in judicial risk assessment by showing all plausible risk categories with guaranteed coverage, enabling judges to see the full range of possibilities rather than just a single point estimate.

Ensuring fair uncertainty quantification across demographic groups in college admissions by verifying that prediction set sizes (number of possible outcomes) are consistent across protected groups, preventing discriminatory overconfidence for certain populations.

limitations.description: Prediction sets can be unnecessarily wide when nonconformity scores vary greatly across the feature space, leading to conservative intervals that reduce practical utility.
Requires a held-out calibration set separate from training data, reducing the amount of data available for model training, which can impact performance on small datasets.
Guarantees only hold under the exchangeability assumption - if test data distribution differs significantly from calibration data, coverage guarantees may be violated.
For multi-class problems, prediction sets may include many classes when the model is uncertain, making decisions difficult when sets contain opposing outcomes.
Computational cost increases with the number of calibration samples, and efficient implementation requires careful design for large-scale or real-time applications.

sample_claims.text: The diagnostic system's prediction sets contain the correct outcome with a guaranteed minimum coverage rate across all patient presentations
The system's uncertainty estimates maintain their specified validity guarantees regardless of the underlying data distribution
The model communicates uncertainty by providing a set of plausible outcomes rather than a single point prediction
The prediction sets achieve equivalent coverage rates across demographic groups without requiring distributional assumptions
The autonomous system's safety-critical predictions are accompanied by statistically guaranteed confidence bounds

name: Platt Scaling
description: Platt scaling turns a classifier's raw scores into calibrated probabilities, meaning that among the cases given a probability of 0.3, about 30 per cent turn out to be positive. It was introduced for support vector machines, whose outputs are distances from a decision boundary rather than probabilities, and applies to any binary classifier that produces a real-valued score. After the classifier is trained, a two-parameter logistic (sigmoid) curve, P(y = 1 | f) = 1 / (1 + exp(A·f + B)), is fitted by maximum likelihood to map each score f to a probability, using labelled cases the classifier was not trained on, taken from a held-out set or from cross-validation folds. The fitted curve is strictly monotonic, so the order of cases and ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve (how well the scores separate the two classes) are unchanged; only the probability attached to each case moves. The output is a recalibrated model, assessed before and after with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and with the Brier score or log loss (two measures of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened).

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's credit-risk team finds that its gradient-boosted default model ranks applicants well but squeezes predicted default probabilities towards the middle of the range. Before the probabilities feed expected-loss provisioning, the team fits Platt scaling on a held-out year of loan outcomes and checks on a reliability diagram that predicted and observed default rates agree in every score decile.

A benefits agency uses a linear support vector machine to flag claims for manual review, but its margin scores mean nothing to caseworkers. The team applies Platt scaling so the review screen can show the probability that a claim needs correcting, publishes the calibration curve in the caseworker guidance, and explains that the figure is a rate across similar claims rather than a verdict on the individual.

limitations.description: The sigmoid shape is an assumption. It corrects the S-shaped distortion typical of support vector machines and boosted trees, whose probabilities bunch towards the middle, but not the reverse distortion of overconfident models such as naive Bayes, whose probabilities pile up near 0 and 1. Where the reliability diagram shows that pattern, a flexible method such as isotonic regression is needed.

It works best when the classifier's scores for the two classes are spread in a similar way (roughly normal with equal variance). In highly imbalanced problems the scores of the two classes do not have equal spread, so the sigmoid can be a poor match for the data.

The curve should be fitted on labelled cases that played no part in training. The classifier separates its own training data better than new data, so a curve fitted to training scores overstates confidence in use; the cost is a held-out calibration set taken from scarce labelled data, or cross-validation with several model fits.

A single curve fitted across the whole population does not make the model calibrated within each subgroup. In a deployed malnutrition-risk model, recalibration improved calibration within each race and sex group, yet intercepts and slopes still differed significantly between Black and White patients. Fitting a curve per group needs group membership at prediction time, which may be unavailable or unlawful to use, and enough labelled cases in every group.

Recalibration changes every probability, so a decision threshold chosen on the raw scores no longer flags the same cases. After logistic recalibration of a deployed malnutrition-risk model, specificity rose from 0.74 to 0.93 and sensitivity fell from 0.75 to 0.35, so the cut-off has to be reset against the cost of each kind of error and the downstream process checked again.

sample_claims.text: After Platt scaling on a held-out year of loan outcomes, the default model's predicted probabilities agree with observed default rates in every score decile, within the tolerance set in the model risk policy.

After Platt scaling, the defect classifier's log loss on the held-out test set is lower than before, and its reliability diagram shows predicted defect rates within the tolerance set in the quality plan.

Each flagged claim is shown to caseworkers with a probability calibrated against held-out review outcomes, and the calibration curve and its meaning are published in the caseworker guidance, so a displayed 30 per cent corresponds to roughly 30 in 100 similar claims needing correction.

name: Temperature Scaling
description: Temperature scaling adjusts a model's confidence by applying a single parameter (temperature) to its predictions. When a model is too confident in its wrong answers, temperature scaling can fix this by making the predictions more realistic. It works by dividing the model's outputs by the temperature value before converting them to probabilities. Higher temperatures make the model less confident, whilst lower temperatures increase confidence. The technique maintains the model's accuracy whilst ensuring that when it says it's 90% confident, it's actually right about 90% of the time.

example_use_cases.description: Adjusting a deep learning image classifier's confidence scores to be realistic, ensuring that when it's 90% confident, it's right 90% of the time.
Making medical diagnosis model predictions more trustworthy by providing realistic confidence scores that doctors can interpret and use to make informed decisions about patient care.

limitations.description: Only addresses calibration at the overall dataset level, not subgroup-specific miscalibration issues.
Does not improve the rank ordering or accuracy of predictions, only adjusts confidence levels.
Assumes that calibration errors are consistent across different types of inputs and feature values.
Requires a separate validation set for temperature parameter optimisation, which may not be available in small datasets.

sample_claims.text: The medical diagnosis system's confidence scores align with observed clinical outcome frequencies across all prediction confidence levels
The credit risk model's probability estimates reflect true default rates without sacrificing discriminative accuracy
The image classifier communicates prediction confidence through calibrated probabilities that match empirical correctness rates
The environmental forecasting model's stated uncertainty levels correspond to actual prediction accuracy across diverse weather conditions

name: Deep Ensembles
description: Deep ensembles combine predictions from multiple neural networks trained independently with different random initializations to capture epistemic uncertainty (model uncertainty). By training several models on the same data with different starting points, the ensemble reveals how much the model's predictions depend on training randomness. The disagreement between ensemble members naturally indicates prediction uncertainty - when models agree, confidence is high; when they disagree, uncertainty is revealed. This approach provides more reliable uncertainty estimates, better out-of-distribution detection, and improved calibration compared to single models.

example_use_cases.description: Improving self-driving car safety by using multiple neural networks to detect obstacles, where disagreement between models signals uncertainty and triggers extra caution or human intervention, providing robust uncertainty quantification for critical decisions.

Communicating prediction confidence to medical professionals by showing the range of diagnoses from multiple trained models, enabling doctors to understand when the AI system is uncertain and requires additional human expertise or testing.

limitations.description: Computationally expensive to train and deploy, requiring multiple complete neural networks which increases training time, memory usage, and inference costs proportionally to ensemble size.
May still provide overconfident predictions for inputs far from the training distribution, as all ensemble members can be similarly confident about out-of-distribution examples.
Requires careful hyperparameter tuning for each ensemble member to ensure diversity, as identical hyperparameters may lead to similar models that reduce uncertainty estimation quality.
Storage and deployment overhead increases linearly with ensemble size, making it challenging to deploy large ensembles in resource-constrained environments or real-time applications.
Ensemble predictions may be difficult to interpret individually, as the final decision emerges from averaging multiple models rather than from a single explainable pathway.

sample_claims.text: The autonomous driving system's predictions are accompanied by confidence estimates that reflect genuine disagreement among multiple independent models
The diagnostic model's uncertainty estimates reveal when different training conditions would yield substantially different predictions
The credit risk model's confidence bounds reflect variability in model structure rather than relying on a single trained configuration

name: Bootstrap Ensembles
description: Bootstrap ensembles estimate how much a model's predictions depend on the particular sample of data it was trained on. The training set is resampled with replacement many times, each resample (a bootstrap replicate) holding as many cases as the original so that some cases are repeated and others left out; one model is trained on each replicate with the same settings, and every new input is passed through all of the models. The spread of the models' predictions for an input, reported as a standard deviation or as a range between percentiles, estimates the uncertainty in the model's prediction for that input, and inputs where the models disagree are those the training data constrain least. The spread covers uncertainty in the fitted model only, not the random variation in individual outcomes, so an interval meant to contain a case's actual outcome must add an estimate of that noise, for example from the models' errors on held-out data. Putting a confidence interval around a measured performance score is a different procedure, which resamples the evaluation set and retrains nothing; see Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics.

example_use_cases.description: An electricity network operator forecasting next-day demand at each substation trains 100 gradient-boosted models on bootstrap replicates of three years of meter readings, resampled in whole-week blocks because consecutive readings are correlated. Planners hold extra reserve at substations where the models' forecasts spread widely, because those are the sites whose forecasts the historical data settle least.

A hospital's readmission-risk tool shows clinicians, beside each patient's predicted risk, the range of risks given by models trained on bootstrap replicates of the training cohort, resampling patients rather than admissions so that one patient's admissions stay together, so that a clinician can see when an estimate rests on few comparable past patients and give it less weight in discharge planning.

A local authority reviewing a housing-need scoring model compares the average spread of bootstrap-ensemble scores across applicant groups and finds it widest for a group with few past applications, which shows that the model's scores for that group are least settled by the data; it collects more cases before letting the scores inform priority for that group.

limitations.description: Every member of the ensemble is a full training run, and every prediction must be made by every member, so training cost, storage and prediction time all grow in proportion to the number of replicates. For large neural networks this usually limits the ensemble to a handful of members, too few for stable percentiles of the spread.

The spread measures uncertainty in the fitted model, not the noise in outcomes. Presented as the range within which a case's actual outcome will fall, it understates the uncertainty, most of all where outcomes are noisy and training data plentiful, so the outcome noise has to be estimated separately, for example from held-out errors, and added.

The spread reflects only what the procedure lets vary: which cases are in each training set and, for models trained from a random start such as neural networks, each member's starting point. Fixed choices such as features, architecture and training settings add no spread. A model consistently wrong for a group the data under-represent can show little spread there, and members can agree closely on inputs unlike the training data, so a small spread is not evidence of reliability.

Each replicate contains on average only about 63 per cent of the distinct training cases, so each member learns from less information than a model trained on all the data. With small datasets or rare classes, some replicates may contain almost none of a rare class or subgroup, which inflates the spread for those cases and can leave individual members unusable.

Resampling single cases assumes they are independent. With repeated measurements of the same person, time series or other grouped data, case resampling spreads related cases across replicates and understates the uncertainty, unless whole groups or time blocks are resampled instead.

sample_claims.text: For each substation's next-day demand forecast, the spread across models trained on bootstrap replicates of the historical data, resampled in whole-week blocks, is reported, and forecasts whose spread exceeds the planning tolerance are flagged.
The flood model's uncertainty for each river gauge reflects how much its predictions change when it is retrained on versions of the gauge records resampled in blocks of consecutive days.
Each readmission-risk score shown to clinicians is accompanied by the range of scores produced by models trained on resampled versions of the training cohort.
The spread of the housing-need model's scores across bootstrap-trained models has been compared between applicant groups and is reported for each group.

name: Jackknife Resampling
description: Jackknife resampling (also called leave-one-out resampling) assesses model stability and uncertainty by systematically removing one data point at a time and retraining the model on the remaining data. Unlike bootstrapping which samples with replacement, jackknife creates n different models by excluding each of the n data points once. This systematic approach reveals how individual points influence results, provides robust estimates of prediction variance, and identifies unusually influential observations that may be outliers or leverage points affecting model reliability.

example_use_cases.description: Evaluating how removing individual countries from a global climate model affects predictions, identifying which regions have outsized influence and providing robust uncertainty estimates for climate projections used in policy decisions.

Providing transparent uncertainty estimates in medical risk prediction by showing how individual patient records influence model predictions, enabling clinicians to understand prediction stability and confidence intervals for treatment decisions.

Ensuring fair model evaluation in hiring algorithms by systematically testing how removing candidates from different demographic groups affects model performance, revealing whether certain populations disproportionately influence the model's behaviour.

limitations.description: Extremely computationally intensive for large datasets, requiring training of n separate models for n data points, making it impractical for datasets with thousands or millions of observations.
May underestimate uncertainty compared to bootstrapping or other resampling methods, as it provides only n different samples rather than a broader exploration of the data distribution.
Assumes that removing single data points provides meaningful insights into model stability, which may not hold when multiple correlated observations drive model behaviour.
Can be sensitive to the choice of performance metric used for evaluation, as different metrics may show different patterns of sensitivity to individual data points.
Provides limited insight into model behaviour on truly novel data, as each jackknife sample is only minimally different from the full training set.

sample_claims.text: The environmental model's uncertainty estimates do not depend on assumptions about sampling distribution or resampling variability
The clinical prediction model's performance stability is quantified by systematically examining the influence of each individual patient record
The credit risk model's predictions are traceable to specific historical loan records that most strongly influence assessment outcomes
The hiring model's performance is not disproportionately dependent on individual candidates from particular demographic groups
The public benefit allocation system identifies individual case records that exert unusual influence on eligibility determinations

name: Cross-validation
description: Cross-validation evaluates model performance and robustness by systematically partitioning data into multiple subsets (folds) and training/testing repeatedly on different combinations. Common approaches include k-fold (splitting into k equal parts), stratified (preserving class distributions), and leave-one-out variants. By testing on multiple independent holdout sets, it reveals how performance varies across different data subsamples, provides robust estimates of generalisation ability, and helps detect overfitting or model instability that single train-test splits might miss.

example_use_cases.description: Using 10-fold cross-validation to estimate a healthcare prediction model's true accuracy and detect overfitting, ensuring robust performance estimates that generalise beyond the specific training sample to new patient populations.

Ensuring fair model evaluation across demographic groups by using stratified cross-validation that maintains representative proportions of protected classes in each fold, revealing whether performance is consistent across different population segments.

limitations.description: Computationally expensive for large datasets or complex models, requiring multiple training runs that scale linearly with the number of folds.
Can provide overly optimistic performance estimates when data has dependencies or structure (e.g., time series, grouped observations) that violate independence assumptions.
May not reflect real-world performance if the training data distribution differs significantly from future deployment conditions or population shifts.
Choice of fold number (k) involves a bias-variance trade-off: fewer folds reduce computational cost but increase variance in estimates, whilst more folds increase computation but may introduce bias.
Standard cross-validation doesn't account for temporal ordering in sequential data, potentially leading to data leakage where future information influences past predictions.

sample_claims.text: The model's performance estimate is robust to the particular train-test partition used
The fraud detection system generalizes consistently across different subsets of historical transaction data
The system maintains equitable performance across demographic groups when evaluated on different data partitions

name: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve
description: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) measures model performance by plotting precision (the proportion of positive predictions that are correct) against recall (the proportion of actual positives that are correctly identified) at various classification thresholds, then calculating the area under the resulting curve. Unlike accuracy or AUC-ROC, AUPRC is particularly valuable for imbalanced datasets where the minority class is of primary interest---a perfect score is 1.0, whilst random performance equals the positive class proportion. By focusing on the precision-recall trade-off, it provides a more informative assessment than overall accuracy for scenarios where false positives and false negatives have different costs, especially when positive examples are rare.

example_use_cases.description: Evaluating fraud detection models where genuine transactions far outnumber fraudulent ones, using AUPRC to optimise the balance between catching fraud (high recall) and minimising false alarms (high precision) for cost-effective operations.

Ensuring fair evaluation of loan default prediction across demographic groups by comparing AUPRC scores, revealing whether models perform equally well at identifying high-risk borrowers regardless of protected characteristics.

limitations.description: More sensitive to class distribution than ROC curves, making it difficult to compare models across datasets with different positive class proportions or to set universal performance thresholds.
Can be overly optimistic on extremely imbalanced datasets where even random predictions may achieve seemingly high AUPRC scores due to the small positive class size.
Provides limited insight into performance at specific operating points, requiring additional analysis to determine optimal threshold selection for deployment.
Interpolation methods for calculating the area under the curve can vary between implementations, potentially leading to slightly different scores for the same model.
Less interpretable than simple metrics like precision or recall at a fixed threshold, making it harder to communicate performance to non-technical stakeholders.

sample_claims.text: The fraud detection model maintains consistent performance at identifying fraudulent transactions across different precision-recall operating points
The model's performance at identifying minority class instances is equitable across demographic groups
The autonomous system's detection capabilities for safety-critical events are robust across different tolerance thresholds for false alarms

name: Safety Envelope Testing
description: Safety envelope testing systematically evaluates AI system performance at the boundaries of its intended operational domain to identify potential failure modes before deployment. The technique involves defining the system's operational design domain (ODD), creating test scenarios that approach or exceed these boundaries, and measuring performance degradation as conditions become more challenging. By testing edge cases, environmental extremes, and boundary conditions, it reveals where the system transitions from safe to unsafe operation, enabling the establishment of clear operational limits and safety margins for deployment.

example_use_cases.description: Testing autonomous vehicle perception systems at the limits of weather conditions, lighting, and sensor coverage to establish safe operational boundaries and determine when human intervention is required.
Evaluating medical AI diagnostic systems with edge cases near decision boundaries to ensure reliable performance and identify when the system should defer to human specialists.
Assessing financial trading algorithms under extreme market conditions and volatility to prevent catastrophic losses and ensure system shutdown protocols activate appropriately.

limitations.description: Requires comprehensive domain expertise to identify relevant boundary conditions and edge cases that could affect system safety.
May be computationally expensive and time-consuming, especially for complex systems with high-dimensional operational domains.
Difficult to achieve complete coverage of all possible boundary conditions, potentially missing critical edge cases.
Results may not generalise to novel scenarios that fall outside the tested boundary conditions.
Establishing appropriate safety thresholds and performance criteria requires careful calibration based on domain-specific risk tolerance.

sample_claims.text: The autonomous vehicle system recognizes when environmental conditions approach the limits of its validated operational envelope and initiates appropriate fallback behaviors
The diagnostic system's performance degradation is characterized across the full range of patient presentation complexity, establishing clear thresholds for specialist referral
The forecasting model maintains quantified accuracy bounds under progressively extreme weather conditions up to documented operational limits
The trading algorithm's decision quality is measured systematically across market volatility conditions, with defined cutoffs for automated trading suspension
The quality control system's inspection reliability has been tested at the boundaries of lighting, part orientation, and surface condition variations expected in production

name: Algorithm Review Boards
description: An algorithm review board is a standing, multidisciplinary body inside an organisation that examines proposed AI systems or AI research projects at set points and decides whether, and on what conditions, they may proceed. The literature also calls these bodies AI ethics boards or AI review boards. They differ from an Institutional Review Board (IRB), which protects the human subjects of research, because they also weigh harms to the people a system will affect and to society. A risk-based triage decides which projects need full review; the project team then submits a written account of the system's purpose, data, foreseeable harms and planned mitigations, and members drawn from technical, legal, ethical and domain backgrounds, sometimes with people from affected communities, question the team and iterate on that account with them. The board approves, approves with conditions such as a monitoring plan or a re-review date, or rejects, and the output is a dated decision record with its reasons and conditions that later reviews and audits can check against what was built.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital group's algorithm review board examines a sepsis early-warning model before a ward pilot. It approves the pilot on condition of a monitoring plan for alert rates and missed cases, names who may switch the model off, and sets a re-review once six months of local performance data are in, before any wider roll-out.

A bank's board reviews a proposed credit-limit model before launch. It asks the team for its disparate-impact analysis by protected group and for evidence that applicants can contest a decision, and withholds approval until both are supplied, so the decision to deploy rests with a body outside the development team.

A university AI research programme releases grant funding only after each project has passed an ethics and society review, in which researchers state the risks their work poses to society and to particular groups, commit to mitigations, and revise them with an interdisciplinary faculty panel.

A government department publishes the board's decision record for a benefits-triage tool, giving the reasons for approval, the conditions attached and the re-review date, so that its oversight committee and the public can see what was examined, by whom and when, and check later that the conditions were met.

limitations.description: Review adds time and cost to every project that goes through it, and organisations under commercial pressure may route work around the board or narrow its remit, so the board's coverage, not just its existence, needs to be shown.

Its judgements are only as good as its membership. A board without the relevant technical, domain or community expertise will miss harms that fall outside what its members know, and a board drawn mainly from inside the team's own reporting line is open to group-think.

Independence is hard to keep inside an organisation. Practitioners report tension between profit and the cost of responsible-AI review, and a board can come under pressure to approve projects that leadership has already committed to, which weakens it most where review matters most.

Without authority to stop or delay a project, and a way to check that its conditions are met, a board's recommendations can be ignored. Evidence from a board is strong only when its decision record shows what it could block and what happened to its conditions.

There is no agreed measure of whether a board works, and review can become box-ticking. A record that a project was reviewed shows that a process ran, not that the review was substantive or that its concerns were addressed.

sample_claims.text: Every high-risk AI system was reviewed and approved by the organisation's algorithm review board before operational use, and the board could have blocked deployment
The conditions the review board attached to the credit-limit model's approval, including a disparate-impact analysis by protected group and a re-review date, were met before and after launch
The clinical decision-support model was deployed under a monitoring plan and re-review schedule set by a multidisciplinary review board independent of the development team
The diagnostic AI system's development and deployment decisions are traceable to dated board decision records that state the risks assessed, the reasons for approval and the conditions attached
The review board's decision record for the risk assessment tool, with its reasons and conditions, is available to the oversight body and the public

name: Red Teaming
description: Red teaming is a structured adversarial evaluation process in which a dedicated team systematically probes an AI/ML system to discover vulnerabilities and failure modes. Unlike individual testing techniques (such as prompt injection testing, jailbreak resistance testing, or safety envelope testing), red teaming defines the organisational methodology: team composition, campaign planning, attack taxonomy, and reporting structure. The red team coordinates diverse attack vectors — including prompt manipulation, adversarial examples, edge case exploitation, and social engineering scenarios — into a coherent assessment programme. Results feed into risk registers and remediation plans rather than pass/fail metrics.

example_use_cases.description: Testing a content moderation AI by attempting to make it generate harmful outputs through creative prompt injection, jailbreaking techniques, and edge case scenarios to identify safety vulnerabilities before deployment.

Probing a medical diagnosis AI system with adversarial examples and edge cases to identify failure modes that could lead to incorrect diagnoses, ensuring the system fails gracefully rather than confidently providing wrong information.

Systematically testing a hiring algorithm with inputs designed to reveal hidden biases, using adversarial examples to check if the system can be manipulated to discriminate against protected groups or favour certain demographics unfairly.

Systematically testing AI systems for security vulnerabilities including prompt injection, data exfiltration, jailbreaking, and model manipulation by simulating adversarial attacks. This helps identify security weaknesses before deployment and provides documented evidence for compliance with regulatory requirements such as EU AI Act Article 55 and ISO 42001 adversarial testing mandates.

limitations.description: Requires highly specialized expertise in both AI/ML systems and adversarial attack methods, making it expensive and difficult to scale across organizations.
Limited by the creativity and knowledge of red team members - can only discover vulnerabilities that testers think to explore, potentially missing novel attack vectors.
Time-intensive process that may not be feasible for rapid development cycles or resource-constrained projects, potentially delaying beneficial system deployments.
May not generalize to real-world adversarial scenarios, as red team attacks may differ significantly from actual malicious use patterns or user behaviours.
Risk of false confidence if red teaming is incomplete or superficial, leading organizations to believe systems are safer than they actually are.

sample_claims.text: The medical AI system maintains safe behavior when subjected to edge case scenarios and adversarial inputs designed to elicit harmful clinical recommendations
The financial advisory system resists attempts to extract confidential client information through social engineering scenarios and multi-turn manipulation strategies
The public benefits allocation system withstands systematic probing designed to reveal exploitable pathways for discriminatory outcomes against protected groups
The autonomous vehicle control system fails gracefully rather than catastrophically when exposed to creative adversarial scenarios that exploit edge cases in perception and decision-making
The conversational AI assistant resists goal misalignment attacks and jailbreak attempts that probe for ways to circumvent safety constraints through iterative prompt refinement

name: Human-in-the-Loop Safeguards
description: Human-in-the-loop safeguards establish systematic checkpoints where human experts review, validate, or override AI/ML system decisions before they take effect. This governance approach combines automated efficiency with human judgement by defining clear intervention criteria (such as uncertainty thresholds, risk levels, or sensitive contexts) that trigger mandatory human oversight. By incorporating domain expertise, ethical considerations, and contextual understanding that machines may lack, these safeguards help ensure that critical decisions maintain appropriate human accountability whilst preserving the benefits of automated processing for routine cases.

example_use_cases.description: Implementing mandatory human physician review for any medical AI diagnostic recommendation before treatment decisions are made, especially for complex cases or when the system confidence is below established thresholds, ensuring patient safety through expert oversight.

Requiring human review of automated loan approval decisions when applicants request explanations or appeal rejections, allowing human underwriters to provide clear reasoning and ensure customers understand the decision-making process behind their application outcomes.

Mandating human oversight when hiring algorithms flag candidates from underrepresented groups for rejection, enabling recruiters to verify that decisions are based on legitimate job-relevant criteria rather than potential algorithmic bias, and providing fair recourse mechanisms.

limitations.description: Scales poorly with high request volumes, creating bottlenecks that can delay critical decisions and potentially overwhelm human reviewers with excessive workload.
Introduces significant latency into automated processes, potentially making time-sensitive applications impractical or reducing user satisfaction with slower response times.
Human reviewers may experience decision fatigue, leading to decreased attention quality over time and potential inconsistency in review standards across different cases or time periods.
Risk of automation bias where humans defer too readily to AI recommendations rather than providing meaningful independent review, undermining the safeguard's effectiveness.
Requires significant ongoing investment in human resources, training, and expertise maintenance, making it expensive to implement and sustain across large-scale systems.

sample_claims.text: The autonomous vehicle system requires qualified driver intervention before executing maneuvers flagged as high-risk by safety criteria
All loan denial decisions are subject to review by qualified underwriters who can access the reasoning behind algorithmic recommendations
The hiring system routes candidates from underrepresented groups to human reviewers when automated scores fall within a defined uncertainty range
The diagnostic support system prevents treatment recommendations from being actioned until reviewed by a licensed physician
The content moderation system escalates borderline cases to human moderators based on defined criteria rather than relying solely on automated classification

name: Confidence Thresholding
description: Confidence thresholding creates decision boundaries based on model uncertainty scores, routing predictions into different handling workflows depending on their confidence levels. High-confidence predictions (e.g., above 95%) proceed automatically, whilst medium-confidence cases (e.g., 70-95%) may trigger additional validation or human review, and low-confidence predictions (below 70%) receive extensive oversight or default to conservative fallback actions. This technique enables organisations to maintain automated efficiency for clear-cut cases whilst ensuring appropriate human intervention for uncertain decisions, balancing operational speed with risk management across safety-critical applications.

example_use_cases.description: Implementing tiered confidence thresholds in autonomous vehicle decision-making where high-confidence lane changes (>98%) execute automatically, medium-confidence decisions (85-98%) trigger additional sensor verification, and low-confidence situations (<85%) engage conservative defensive driving modes or request human takeover.

Deploying confidence thresholding in fraud detection systems where high-confidence legitimate transactions (>90%) process immediately, medium-confidence cases (70-90%) undergo additional automated checks, and low-confidence transactions (<70%) require human analyst review, ensuring system reliability through graduated response mechanisms.

Using confidence thresholds in automated loan decisions to provide clear explanations to applicants, where high-confidence approvals include simple explanations, medium-confidence decisions provide detailed reasoning about key factors, and low-confidence cases receive comprehensive explanations with guidance on potential improvements.

limitations.description: Many models produce poorly calibrated confidence scores that don't accurately reflect true prediction uncertainty, leading to overconfident predictions for incorrect outputs or underconfident scores for correct predictions.

Threshold selection requires careful calibration and domain expertise, as inappropriate thresholds can either overwhelm human reviewers with too many cases or miss genuinely uncertain decisions that need oversight.

High-confidence predictions may still be incorrect or harmful, particularly when models encounter adversarial inputs, out-of-distribution data, or systematic biases that the confidence mechanism doesn't detect.
Static thresholds may become inappropriate over time as model performance degrades, data distribution shifts occur, or operational contexts change, requiring ongoing monitoring and adjustment.

Implementation complexity increases significantly when managing multiple confidence levels and routing mechanisms, potentially introducing system failures or inconsistencies in how different confidence ranges are handled.

sample_claims.text: The autonomous system transitions to conservative fallback modes when prediction confidence falls below established operational thresholds
The system routes low-confidence predictions to human review while processing high-confidence cases automatically
The fraud detection system applies graduated verification steps based on transaction confidence levels
The diagnostic system communicates the level of certainty alongside each prediction to support clinical decision-making
The automated decision system engages additional safeguards when operating in regions of high uncertainty

name: Runtime Monitoring and Circuit Breakers
description: Runtime monitoring and circuit breakers watch a deployed AI system's operational and model-level signals and automatically stop, limit or reroute calls to the model when those signals cross preset limits. The circuit breaker, a software resilience pattern, wraps calls to the model: while closed it passes requests through and counts failures in a rolling time window; when failures pass a threshold it opens, so further requests fail at once or receive a fallback such as a cached answer, a simpler model, a rule-based default or referral to a person; after a cooldown it half-opens and lets a few trial requests through, closing again only if they succeed. For a machine learning model, what counts as a failure is widened from errors and timeouts to model-level signals available at the moment of prediction, such as input drift scores, low prediction confidence, out-of-range outputs or limits on the actions the system may take, because true accuracy usually cannot be measured until outcomes arrive later. The output is a log of breaker state changes, the metrics that triggered them and the alerts raised, which shows when and why the system was restricted; the protection is only as good as the chosen thresholds and the fallback behind the breaker.

example_use_cases.description: Implementing circuit breakers in a medical AI system that automatically halt diagnosis recommendations if prediction confidence drops below 85%, error rates exceed 2%, or response times increase beyond acceptable limits, preventing potentially harmful misdiagnoses during system degradation.
