Deploying runtime monitoring for a recommendation engine that tracks recommendation diversity, click-through rates, and user engagement patterns, automatically switching to simpler algorithms when complex models show signs of performance degradation or unusual behaviour patterns.

Establishing transparent monitoring dashboards for a loan approval system that display real-time metrics on approval rates across demographic groups, processing times, and model confidence levels, enabling stakeholders to verify consistent and fair operation.

limitations.description: Threshold calibration requires extensive domain expertise and historical data analysis, as overly sensitive settings trigger excessive false alarms whilst conservative thresholds may miss genuine system failures.
False positive alerts can unnecessarily disrupt service availability and user experience, potentially causing more harm than the issues they aim to prevent, especially in time-sensitive applications.
Sophisticated attacks or gradual performance degradation may operate within normal metric ranges, evading detection by staying below established thresholds whilst still causing cumulative damage.

Monitoring infrastructure introduces additional complexity and potential failure points, requiring robust implementation to avoid situations where the monitoring system itself becomes a source of system instability.
High-frequency monitoring and circuit breaker mechanisms can add computational overhead and latency to system operations, potentially impacting performance in resource-constrained environments.

sample_claims.text: The diagnostic system automatically halts prediction generation when monitored accuracy metrics fall below operational safety thresholds
The autonomous vehicle system engages protective failover mechanisms when sensor input quality or processing latency deviates from validated operational envelopes
The fraud detection service maintains continuous operation by automatically throttling request rates when system response times exceed acceptable performance bounds
The forecasting model prevents cascading failures by automatically switching to fallback algorithms when prediction error rates or resource consumption patterns exceed established limits
The system provides stakeholders with real-time visibility into operational health metrics and protective action triggering events

name: Model Cards
description: Model cards are standardised documentation frameworks that systematically document machine learning models through structured templates. The templates cover intended use cases, performance metrics across different demographic groups and operating conditions, training data characteristics, evaluation procedures, limitations, and ethical considerations. They serve as comprehensive technical specifications that enable informed model selection, prevent inappropriate deployment, support regulatory compliance, and facilitate fair assessment by providing transparent reporting of model capabilities and constraints across diverse populations and scenarios.

example_use_cases.description: Documenting a medical diagnosis AI with detailed performance metrics across different patient demographics, age groups, and clinical conditions, enabling healthcare providers to understand when the model should be trusted and when additional expert consultation is needed for patient safety.

Creating comprehensive model cards for hiring algorithms that transparently report performance differences across demographic groups, helping HR departments identify potential bias issues and ensure equitable candidate evaluation processes.

Publishing detailed model documentation for a credit scoring API that clearly describes training data sources, evaluation methodologies, and performance limitations, enabling financial institutions to make informed decisions about model deployment and regulatory compliance.

limitations.description: Creating comprehensive model cards requires substantial time, expertise, and resources to gather performance data across diverse conditions and demographic groups, potentially delaying model deployment timelines.
Information can become outdated quickly as models are retrained, updated, or deployed in new contexts, requiring ongoing maintenance and version control to remain accurate and useful.
Organisations may provide incomplete or superficial documentation to avoid revealing competitive advantages or potential liabilities, undermining the transparency goals of model cards.
Lack of standardised formats and enforcement mechanisms means model card quality and completeness vary significantly across different organisations and use cases.
Technical complexity of documenting model behaviour across all relevant dimensions may exceed the expertise of some development teams, leading to gaps in critical information.

sample_claims.text: The model's performance characteristics are documented across all relevant demographic groups and operating conditions
The diagnostic system's accuracy and error rates are reported separately for each patient subpopulation
The model's intended use cases and known limitations are clearly communicated to decision-makers
The lending model's approval rates and error distributions are transparently reported for all applicant demographics
The system's training data characteristics, evaluation procedures, and ethical considerations are comprehensively documented

name: Datasheets for Datasets
description: Datasheets for datasets establish comprehensive documentation standards for datasets, systematically recording creation methodology, data composition, collection procedures, preprocessing transformations, intended applications, potential biases, privacy considerations, and maintenance protocols. These structured documents enhance dataset transparency by providing essential context for appropriate usage, enabling informed decisions about dataset suitability for specific tasks, supporting bias detection and mitigation efforts, ensuring compliance with data protection regulations, and promoting responsible data stewardship throughout the entire data lifecycle from collection to disposal.

example_use_cases.description: Documenting a medical imaging dataset with detailed information about patient privacy protections, anonymisation procedures, and data sharing constraints to ensure sensitive health information is handled appropriately and regulatory compliance is maintained.

Creating comprehensive datasheets for recruitment datasets that document demographic representation across different job categories, helping developers identify potential bias in training data and develop more equitable hiring algorithms.

Establishing transparent documentation for financial transaction datasets that clearly describes data collection methodology, preprocessing steps, and intended use cases, enabling researchers to make informed decisions about dataset appropriateness for their specific applications.

Documenting a safety-critical autonomous vehicle perception dataset with records of sensor calibration procedures, environmental conditions during collection, edge-case scenario coverage, and known distributional gaps, enabling safety engineers to assess whether training data adequately represents the operating conditions required for safe deployment and to support regulatory type-approval submissions.

Documenting the statistical distributions, temporal coverage, and known quality characteristics of training datasets to support model monitoring pipelines, enabling operations teams to detect data drift and assess whether production data remains within the documented training distribution for informed decisions about model retraining or recalibration.

limitations.description: Creating thorough datasheets requires significant time investment and domain expertise to properly document collection methods, biases, and ethical considerations, potentially delaying dataset release or publication.
Information may become outdated as datasets undergo preprocessing, cleaning, or augmentation, requiring ongoing maintenance to ensure documentation accuracy throughout the data lifecycle.
Absence of standardised templates and enforcement mechanisms leads to inconsistent documentation quality and completeness across different organisations and research communities.
Dataset creators may intentionally omit sensitive information about collection methods, participant consent, or potential biases to avoid legal liability or competitive disadvantage.
Limited adoption and awareness means many existing datasets lack proper documentation, creating gaps in the historical record and making legacy dataset assessment difficult.

sample_claims.text: The training dataset's collection methodology, participant consent procedures, and intended use constraints are documented and accessible to model developers
The dataset composition across demographic groups and protected characteristics is documented to enable bias detection during model development
The dataset's privacy protections, anonymisation procedures, and re-identification risks are documented before data sharing
The data provenance from original sources through preprocessing transformations is traceable for regulatory review
The environmental sensing dataset documents geographic coverage, temporal distribution, and known measurement biases across different operating conditions

name: MLflow Experiment Tracking
description: MLflow is an open-source platform that tracks machine learning experiments by automatically logging parameters, metrics, models, and artifacts throughout the ML lifecycle. It provides a centralised repository for comparing different experimental runs, reproducing results, and managing model versions. Teams can track hyperparameters, evaluation metrics, model files, and execution environment details, creating a comprehensive audit trail that supports collaboration, reproducibility, and regulatory compliance across the entire machine learning development process.

example_use_cases.description: Tracking medical diagnosis model experiments across different hospitals, logging hyperparameters, performance metrics, and model artifacts to ensure reproducible research and enable regulatory audits of model development processes.

Managing fraud detection model versions in production, tracking which specific model configuration and training data version is deployed, enabling quick rollback and performance comparison when system reliability issues arise.

Documenting loan approval model experiments with complete parameter tracking and performance logging across demographic groups, supporting fair lending compliance by providing transparent records of model development and validation processes.

limitations.description: Requires teams to adopt disciplined logging practices and may introduce overhead to development workflows if not properly integrated into existing processes.
Storage costs can grow substantially with extensive artifact logging, especially for large models or high-frequency experimentation.
Tracking quality depends on developers consistently logging relevant information, with incomplete logging leading to gaps in experimental records.
Complex multi-stage pipelines may require custom instrumentation to capture dependencies and data flow relationships effectively.
Security and access control configurations require careful setup to protect sensitive model information and experimental data in shared environments.

sample_claims.text: All experimental configurations and hyperparameters tested during model development are centrally logged with their corresponding performance outcomes
The deployed clinical model is reproducible from logged training parameters, data versions, and execution environment specifications
The fraud detection model's performance evolution across successive training runs is traceable through logged metrics and artifact histories
The production model version can be systematically compared against alternative experimental configurations evaluated during development
Model training artifacts and evaluation metrics are accessible to authorized team members through a centralized repository supporting collaborative review

name: Data Version Control
description: Data Version Control (DVC) is a Git-like version control system specifically designed for machine learning data, models, and experiments. It tracks changes to large data files, maintains reproducible ML pipelines, and creates a complete audit trail of data transformations, model training, and evaluation processes. DVC works alongside Git to provide end-to-end lineage tracking from raw data through preprocessing, training, and deployment, enabling teams to reproduce any model version and understand exactly how datasets evolved throughout the ML lifecycle.

example_use_cases.description: Tracking medical imaging dataset versions and model training pipelines to ensure reproducible research results, enabling hospitals to verify which specific data version and preprocessing steps were used for regulatory submissions.

Managing credit scoring model data pipelines with complete version control of training datasets, feature engineering steps, and model artifacts, ensuring reliable model reproduction and rollback capabilities when performance issues arise.

Maintaining pharmaceutical drug discovery data lineage across multiple research teams, tracking compound datasets, feature extraction processes, and model versions to support FDA submissions with complete experimental provenance.

limitations.description: Requires learning Git-like workflows and CLI commands, which may have a steep learning curve for teams unfamiliar with version control systems.
Storage costs can be substantial for large datasets with frequent changes, especially when maintaining multiple versions and branches of data.
Complex data pipelines with many interdependencies may require significant setup time and careful configuration to track properly.
Performance can degrade with very large files or datasets due to checksumming and synchronisation overhead during operations.
Team coordination becomes essential as improper branch management or merge conflicts can disrupt collaborative workflows.

sample_claims.text: The training dataset's lineage is traceable from original data sources through all preprocessing transformations to the deployed model
The model's performance can be recreated using the exact dataset version and pipeline configuration from any prior release
All modifications to sensor calibration data and feature extraction steps are documented with timestamps and author attribution
The system can be rolled back to any previous data processing pipeline version when performance degradation is detected
The complete history of dataset changes is preserved and queryable across the model's development lifecycle

name: Monotonicity Constraints
description: Monotonicity constraints enforce consistent directional relationships between input features and model predictions, ensuring that increasing a feature value either always increases, always decreases, or has no effect on the output. These constraints integrate domain knowledge into model training, preventing counterintuitive relationships that may arise from spurious correlations in data. By maintaining logical feature relationships (e.g., experience always positively influences salary), monotonicity constraints enhance model trustworthiness, interpretability, and alignment with business logic whilst often improving generalisation to new data.

example_use_cases.description: Enforcing that a mortgage approval model always treats higher income, longer employment history, and higher credit scores as positive factors, making the decision logic transparent and intuitive for loan officers and applicants whilst preventing counterintuitive relationships that could undermine trust in the system.

Constraining a healthcare cost prediction model so that age and number of chronic conditions always increase predicted costs, ensuring the model generalises reliably to new patient populations and maintains logical behaviour even when training data contains sampling biases or unusual correlations.

Implementing monotonic constraints in an insurance premium model where driving experience always reduces premiums and accident history always increases them, creating consistent pricing logic that regulatory authorities can easily validate and customers can understand and trust.

limitations.description: Can reduce model accuracy when real-world relationships are inherently non-monotonic, such as the inverted-U relationship between experience and performance, where constraints force oversimplified linear relationships.

Requires substantial domain expertise to identify which features should have monotonic relationships, creating dependency on subject matter experts and potential for incorrect constraint specification.
Increases computational complexity during training as optimisation algorithms must respect additional constraints, potentially leading to longer training times and convergence difficulties.
May mask important non-linear patterns in data that could be crucial for understanding system behaviour, particularly in exploratory analysis where discovering unexpected relationships is valuable.

Limited applicability to certain model types, with implementation varying significantly across algorithms (well-supported in tree-based models, more complex in neural networks), restricting technique flexibility.

sample_claims.text: The lending model's approval probability increases consistently with applicant income without counterintuitive reversals
The insurance premium calculation respects logical directional relationships where risk factors monotonically increase costs
The clinical risk assessment maintains consistent directionality where deteriorating vital signs monotonically increase predicted severity
The energy consumption forecast ensures that increased building occupancy always raises predicted demand
The hiring suitability score preserves expected relationships where relevant experience monotonically improves candidate ratings

name: Generalized Additive Models
description: An intrinsically interpretable modelling technique that extends linear models by allowing flexible, nonlinear relationships between individual features and the target whilst maintaining the additive structure that preserves transparency. Each feature's effect is modelled separately as a smooth function, visualised as a curve showing how the feature influences predictions across its range. GAMs achieve this through spline functions or other smoothing techniques that capture complex patterns in individual variables without interactions, making them particularly valuable for domains requiring both predictive accuracy and model interpretability.

example_use_cases.description: Predicting hospital readmission risk with a GAM that provides transparent, auditable risk assessments by showing how readmission probability varies nonlinearly with patient age, blood pressure, and medication adherence, enabling clinicians to understand and trust the model's reasoning for regulatory compliance.

Building a credit scoring model that explains loan decisions to applicants by visualising how income, credit history, and debt-to-income ratio individually affect approval likelihood, providing clear feature attributions that satisfy fair lending requirements and regulatory explainability mandates.

limitations.description: Cannot capture complex interactions between features unless explicitly modelled, limiting their ability to represent relationships where variables influence each other.
Setup requires domain expertise to decide which features need nonlinear treatment and appropriate smoothing parameters, making model specification more challenging than linear models.
Fitting process is computationally more expensive than linear models, particularly for large datasets with many features requiring smoothing.
Risk of overfitting individual feature relationships if smoothing parameters are not properly regularised, potentially reducing generalisation performance.
Interpretation complexity increases with the number of nonlinear features, as understanding multiple smooth curves simultaneously becomes cognitively demanding.

sample_claims.text: The clinical decision model's predictions are decomposable into individual feature contributions that can be visualized as smooth curves
The lending model reveals how each applicant attribute nonlinearly influences approval likelihood whilst maintaining an additive structure
The model's decision logic is directly inspectable without requiring separate explanation methods
The resource allocation model documents how each policy-relevant factor shapes outcomes through interpretable functional relationships

name: Neuron Activation Analysis
description: Neuron activation analysis examines the firing patterns of individual neurons in neural networks by probing them with diverse inputs and analysing their activation responses. This technique helps understand what concepts, features, or patterns different neurons have learned to recognise, providing insights into the model's internal representations. For large language models, this can reveal neurons specialised for linguistic concepts, semantic categories, or even potentially harmful patterns, enabling targeted interventions and deeper model understanding.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing GPT-based models to identify specific neurons that activate on toxic or harmful content, enabling targeted interventions to reduce model toxicity whilst preserving general language capabilities for safer AI deployment.

Examining activation patterns in multilingual language models to detect neurons that exhibit systematic biases when processing text from different linguistic communities, revealing implicit representation inequalities that could affect downstream applications.

Investigating individual neurons in medical language models to understand which clinical concepts and medical knowledge representations drive diagnostic suggestions, enabling healthcare professionals to validate the model's medical reasoning pathways.

limitations.description: Many neurons exhibit polysemantic behaviour, representing multiple unrelated concepts simultaneously, making it difficult to assign clear interpretable meanings to individual neural units.
Important model behaviours are often distributed across many neurons rather than localised in single units, requiring analysis of neural circuits and interactions that can be exponentially complex.

Computational costs scale dramatically with modern large language models containing billions of parameters, making comprehensive neuron-by-neuron analysis prohibitively expensive for complete model understanding.

Neuron activation patterns are highly context-dependent, with the same neuron potentially serving different roles based on surrounding input context, complicating consistent interpretation across diverse scenarios.
Interpretation of activation patterns often relies on subjective human analysis without rigorous validation methods, potentially leading to confirmation bias or misattribution of neural functions.

sample_claims.text: The language model's internal representations reveal which individual computational units respond to specific semantic concepts relevant to clinical diagnosis
The content moderation system's harmful output patterns are attributable to identifiable neurons that can be selectively modified without degrading general language capabilities
The multilingual model's neurons do not exhibit systematic activation biases when processing text from different linguistic communities
The financial risk assessment model's internal computational units encode interpretable market concepts rather than opaque statistical artifacts
The model's specialized neurons for toxic content detection activate consistently across diverse phrasings and contexts of harmful patterns

name: Prompt Robustness Testing
description: Prompt robustness testing measures how much a language model's answers, or its performance on a task, change when the prompt is varied in ways that should not matter: rewording an instruction, changing formatting, punctuation or capitalisation, reordering elements, or introducing the typos and synonym swaps real users make. The tester starts from a set of task prompts with known correct answers, generates variants of each that keep its meaning, either from templates of plausible formats or with automated perturbation tools such as PromptBench, and runs the model on every variant. The result is reported as the spread of performance across variants, for example the gap between the best and worst format or the drop in accuracy under perturbation, together with the variants that changed the answer. Reporting the spread rather than one score matters because results from a single prompt template are brittle: on one widely used open model, accuracy differed by up to 76 points across formatting changes that kept the meaning.

example_use_cases.description: A digital health provider testing a symptom-triage chatbot rewrites each benchmark scenario as a brief layperson message, a detailed account, a clinician's summary and an anxious message, and checks that the urgency category stays the same across all four, treating any change as a failure to investigate before release.

A public-sector team choosing between candidate language models for classifying citizen enquiries evaluates each across a set of plausible prompt formats and instruction paraphrases, and compares models on worst-format and average accuracy rather than on a single prompt, because the ranking of models can change with the template.

A bank validating a model that summarises suspicious-transaction reports checks that the risk category it extracts does not change when the same activity is described with different terminology, abbreviations or layout, as reports from different branches would be.

A support team testing a request-routing model varies one element of each request at a time to separate the words that change the routing decision from formatting changes that should not, and uses the result to write guidance on how customers should phrase requests.

limitations.description: The space of possible prompt variants is unbounded, so a test samples it. A model can pass on every variant tried and still fail on a phrasing nobody generated, and the conclusion holds only for the kinds of variation the test set covers.

Whether a variant keeps the meaning of the original is a judgement. Automated perturbations such as typos and synonym swaps can change meaning or produce text no user would write, especially in specialised language, so variant sets need checking by someone who knows the domain.

Results do not transfer between models: which formats work well correlated only weakly across models in a large study, and robustness to one domain's phrasing says little about another's. The test has to be rerun for each model version, each prompt template change and each domain.

Every variant multiplies the number of model calls, and for open-ended answers each response may need scoring by a domain expert rather than against a fixed label. Testing many formats across many examples and candidate models quickly becomes costly.

It shows that outputs are brittle, not why. Choosing the best-scoring template on the same variants used to test it gives an optimistic estimate of how that template will perform on new inputs, so template selection and the final robustness measurement need separate data.

sample_claims.text: The triage assistant assigns the same urgency category to each benchmark scenario whether the patient's description is brief, detailed, clinical or anxious in style
The enquiry-classification model's accuracy stays within a stated margin of its mean across every prompt template and instruction paraphrase in the evaluation set
The risk category extracted from suspicious-transaction reports does not change when the same activity is described with different terminology or layout
The changes that alter the routing model's decisions have been identified and are changes to the content of a request, not to its formatting

name: Causal Mediation Analysis in Language Models
description: Causal mediation analysis in language models is a mechanistic interpretability technique that systematically investigates how specific internal components (neurons, attention heads, or layers) causally contribute to model outputs. By performing controlled interventions—such as activating, deactivating, or modifying specific components—researchers can trace the causal pathways through which information flows and transforms within the model. This approach goes beyond correlation to establish causal relationships, enabling researchers to understand not just what features influence outputs, but how and why they do so through specific computational pathways.

example_use_cases.description: Investigating causal pathways in content moderation models to understand how specific attention mechanisms contribute to flagging potentially harmful content, enabling verification that safety decisions rely on appropriate features rather than spurious correlations and ensuring robust content filtering.

Tracing causal pathways in large language models performing mathematical reasoning tasks to understand how intermediate steps are computed and stored, revealing which components are responsible for different aspects of logical inference and enabling validation of reasoning processes.

limitations.description: Requires sophisticated understanding of model architecture to design meaningful interventions, as poorly chosen intervention points may yield misleading causal conclusions or fail to capture relevant computational pathways.

Results are highly dependent on the validity of underlying causal assumptions, which can be difficult to verify in complex, high-dimensional neural network spaces where multiple causal pathways may interact.

Comprehensive causal analysis requires extensive computational resources, particularly for large models, as each intervention requires separate forward passes and multiple intervention combinations for robust conclusions.

Distinguishing between direct causal effects and indirect effects mediated through other components can be challenging, potentially leading to oversimplified causal narratives that miss important intermediate processes.

Causal relationships identified in specific contexts or datasets may not generalise to different domains, tasks, or model versions, requiring careful validation across diverse scenarios to ensure robust findings.

sample_claims.text: The language model's outputs are traceable to specific internal computational pathways rather than distributed correlations
The content moderation system's flagging decisions depend on appropriate features through verifiable causal mechanisms
The model's reasoning process flows through identifiable intermediate representations that can be independently validated
The system's harmful output generation is attributable to specific intervening mechanisms that can be isolated and addressed

name: Concept Activation Vectors
description: Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs), also known as Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV), identify mathematical directions in neural network representation space that correspond to human-understandable concepts such as 'stripes', 'young', or 'medical equipment'. The technique works by finding linear directions that separate activations of concept examples from non-concept examples, then measuring how much these concept directions influence the model's predictions. This provides quantitative answers to questions like 'How much does the concept of youth affect this model's hiring decisions?' enabling systematic bias detection and model understanding.

example_use_cases.description: Auditing a medical imaging model to verify it focuses on diagnostic features (like 'tumour characteristics') rather than irrelevant concepts (like 'scanner type' or 'patient positioning') when classifying chest X-rays, ensuring clinical decisions rely on medically relevant information.

Testing whether a hiring algorithm's resume screening decisions are influenced by concepts related to protected characteristics such as 'gender-associated names', 'prestigious universities', or 'employment gaps', enabling systematic bias detection and compliance verification.

Providing regulatory-compliant explanations for financial lending decisions by quantifying how concepts like 'debt-to-income ratio', 'employment stability', and 'credit history length' influence loan approval models, with precise sensitivity scores for audit documentation.

limitations.description: Requires clearly defined concept examples and non-concept examples, which can be challenging to obtain for abstract or subjective concepts.
Assumes that meaningful concept directions exist as linear separable directions in the model's internal representation space, which may not hold for all concepts.
Results depend heavily on which network layer is examined, as different layers capture different levels of abstraction and concept representation.
Computational cost grows significantly with model size and number of concepts tested, though recent advances like FastCAV address this limitation.
Interpretation requires domain expertise to define meaningful concepts and understand the significance of sensitivity scores in practical contexts.

sample_claims.text: The model's classification decisions are quantifiably linked to human-interpretable concepts rather than opaque internal representations
The hiring system's candidate evaluations are demonstrably independent of concepts associated with protected characteristics
The diagnostic model's sensitivity to clinically relevant concepts is documented with quantitative influence scores
The credit assessment model's reliance on demographic-related concepts is measurable and within acceptable bounds
The vision system's object recognition depends on semantically meaningful visual concepts aligned with domain expertise

name: Reweighing
description: Reweighing is a pre-processing method, from Kamiran and Calders (2012), that removes the statistical association between a protected attribute and the outcome label in training data by giving each training example a weight, without changing any feature values or labels. For every combination of group and label (for example, women who were hired), the weight is the number of examples that combination would have if group and label were independent, divided by the number it actually has: the group's share of the data times the label's share, over the combination's observed share. Combinations rarer than independence predicts, such as positive outcomes in a disadvantaged group, are weighted up and over-represented ones are weighted down, so that in the weighted data every group has the same rate of positive labels. A model is then trained on the original data using these weights; the outputs are the weighted training set and a small table of weights that records exactly how each group-label combination was adjusted.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model team finds that in the historical loan decisions used as training labels, applicants from one ethnic group were approved far less often than others. Before retraining its approval model it computes reweighing weights, so that approved applicants from that group count for more and refused ones for less, trains with them as sample weights, and compares the approval-rate gap and accuracy on held-out data against the unweighted model.

A health insurer's analytics team building a model to target postpartum depression outreach from Medicaid claims compares reweighing by race with simply removing race from the inputs. It reports each option's disparate impact ratio (the ratio of positive-prediction rates between groups) and predictive performance to its clinical governance group before choosing one.

A recruitment platform training a shortlisting model on past hiring outcomes, in which women were hired into senior engineering roles less often than men, applies reweighing by sex before training so that the weighted history shows equal hiring rates, then checks shortlisting rates by sex on a held-out set of applications.

An auditor reviewing a benefits-fraud model asks for the table of reweighing weights kept with the training run. A weight of 1.8 on one nationality group's not-fraud cases shows how far that group's historical labels departed from independence, and the table records exactly how the training data were adjusted, so the auditor can reconstruct the intervention without rerunning it.

limitations.description: Its target is fixed: equal rates of positive labels across groups in the weighted training data (statistical parity). It does not aim at equal error rates such as equal opportunity, and the weights are computed once, before training, so they cannot respond to where the trained model actually errs. An adaptive variant (Krasanakis et al., 2018) re-estimates weights during training for error-rate criteria, but it has no maintained implementation.

It removes all association between group and label, including any part a legitimate factor explains. Kamiran and Calders give the example of car insurance, where more accidents among men may justify different outcomes by sex; reweighing erases that difference too, so it over-corrects wherever some gap between groups is warranted.

The learning algorithm must accept example weights; where it cannot, the data have to be resampled instead, which is a different method. Only the training data are balanced, so the trained model's predictions are not guaranteed to be: outcome rates by group must be measured on held-out data after training rather than assumed.

When a group-label combination is rare its weight is large (a combination with a tenth of its expected count gets a weight of ten), so a handful of examples can dominate training. This raises variance and amplifies any labelling errors in exactly the group the method is meant to protect, and it bites hardest with small or intersectional groups.

sample_claims.text: The approval model was trained on loan history reweighed so that every ethnic group has the same approval rate in the weighted data, and its approval-rate gap on held-out applicants is reported alongside its accuracy.
The postpartum depression outreach model, trained with reweighing by race, has a disparate impact ratio within the agreed range on held-out patients.
The shortlisting model's training data were reweighed by sex before training, and shortlisting rates by sex on held-out applications fall within the agreed tolerance.

The adjustment made to the fraud model's training data is recorded as a table of weights for each group and label, kept with the training run, from which an auditor can reconstruct how the data were changed.

name: Disparate Impact Remover
description: Disparate Impact Remover is a preprocessing technique that transforms feature values in a dataset to reduce statistical dependence between features and protected attributes (like race or gender). The method modifies non-protected features through mathematical transformations that preserve the utility of the data whilst reducing correlations that could lead to discriminatory outcomes. This approach specifically targets the '80% rule' disparate impact threshold by adjusting feature distributions to ensure more equitable treatment across demographic groups in downstream model predictions.

example_use_cases.description: Transforming features in a credit scoring dataset where variables like 'years of employment' and 'education level' are correlated with race, applying mathematical transformations to reduce these correlations whilst preserving the predictive value for creditworthiness assessment.

Preprocessing a recruitment dataset where features like 'previous job titles' and 'university attended' correlate with gender, modifying these features to ensure the '80% rule' is met whilst maintaining useful information for predicting job performance.

limitations.description: Feature transformations may reduce model accuracy by removing or distorting important predictive information during the debiasing process.
Only addresses measured protected attributes and cannot eliminate bias that operates through unmeasured proxy variables.
Effectiveness depends on the specific transformation method chosen and may not generalise well to different datasets or domains.
May create artificial feature distributions that don't reflect real-world data patterns, potentially causing issues in model deployment.

sample_claims.text: The model's input features exhibit reduced statistical dependence on protected demographic attributes
The credit assessment system meets the 80% rule threshold for equitable treatment across demographic groups
The lending model's feature transformations preserve creditworthiness information whilst reducing demographic correlations

name: Fairness GAN
description: A data generation technique that employs Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to create fair synthetic datasets by learning to generate data representations that preserve utility whilst obfuscating protected attributes. Unlike traditional GANs, Fairness GANs incorporate fairness constraints into the training objective, ensuring that the generated data maintains statistical parity across demographic groups. The technique can be used for data augmentation to balance underrepresented groups or to create privacy-preserving synthetic datasets that remove demographic bias from training data.

example_use_cases.description: Generating balanced synthetic datasets for medical research by creating additional samples from underrepresented demographic groups, ensuring equal representation across ethnicity and gender whilst maintaining the statistical properties needed for robust model training.

limitations.description: GAN training is notoriously difficult to stabilise, with potential for mode collapse or failure to converge, especially when additional fairness constraints are imposed.
Ensuring fairness in generated data may come at the cost of data utility, potentially reducing the quality or realism of synthetic samples.
Requires large datasets to train both generator and discriminator networks effectively, limiting applicability in data-scarce domains.
Evaluation complexity is high, as it requires assessing both the quality of generated data and the preservation of fairness properties across demographic groups.
May inadvertently introduce new biases if the fairness constraints are not properly specified or if the training data itself contains subtle biases.

sample_claims.text: The training dataset maintains balanced representation across demographic groups without compromising the statistical properties needed for model generalization
The generated dataset exhibits statistical parity across protected attributes without relying on direct attribute removal
The recommendation system's training data contains equitable representation of user demographics through controlled synthetic augmentation

name: Relabelling
description: A preprocessing fairness technique that modifies class labels in training data to achieve equal positive outcome rates across protected groups. Also known as 'data massaging', this method identifies instances that contribute to discriminatory patterns and flips their labels (from positive to negative or vice versa) to balance the proportion of positive outcomes between demographic groups. The technique aims to remove historical bias from training data whilst preserving the overall class distribution, enabling standard classifiers to learn from discrimination-free datasets.

example_use_cases.description: Preprocessing historical hiring datasets by relabelling borderline cases to ensure equal hiring rates across gender and ethnicity groups, correcting for past discriminatory practices whilst maintaining overall qualification standards for fair recruitment model training.

Creating transparent credit scoring datasets by documenting which loan applications had labels modified to address historical lending discrimination, providing clear audit trails showing how training data bias was systematically corrected before model development.

limitations.description: Altering training labels risks introducing new biases or artificial patterns that may not reflect genuine relationships in the data.
Deciding which instances to relabel requires careful selection criteria and domain expertise to avoid inappropriate label changes.
May reduce prediction accuracy if too many labels are changed, particularly when the modifications conflict with genuine patterns in the data.
Requires access to ground truth or expert knowledge to determine whether original labels reflect genuine outcomes or discriminatory bias.
Effectiveness depends on accurate identification of discriminatory instances, which can be challenging when bias patterns are subtle or complex.

sample_claims.text: The hiring system's training data has been corrected to achieve equal qualification acceptance rates across demographic groups through systematic label modification
The training dataset documents which diagnostic labels were modified to correct for historical treatment bias in underrepresented patient populations
The model was trained on corrected labels that remove discriminatory patterns from historical outcomes without altering the underlying feature distributions
The preprocessing pipeline identifies and flips classification labels for borderline cases to balance positive outcome rates across protected groups before model training

name: Preferential Sampling
description: A preprocessing fairness technique developed by Kamiran and Calders that addresses dataset imbalances by re-sampling training data with preference for underrepresented groups to achieve discrimination-free classification. This method modifies the training distribution by prioritising borderline objects (instances near decision boundaries) from underrepresented groups for duplication whilst potentially removing instances from overrepresented groups. Unlike relabelling approaches, preferential sampling maintains original class labels whilst creating a more balanced dataset that prevents models from learning biased patterns due to skewed group representation.

example_use_cases.description: Preprocessing hiring datasets by preferentially sampling candidates from underrepresented gender and ethnic groups, particularly focusing on borderline cases near decision boundaries, to ensure fair representation whilst maintaining original qualifications and labels for unbiased recruitment model training.

Creating transparent credit scoring datasets by documenting and adjusting the sampling process to ensure equal representation across demographic groups, providing clear evidence to regulators that training data imbalances have been addressed without altering original creditworthiness labels.

limitations.description: Oversampling minority groups can cause overfitting to duplicated examples, particularly when borderline instances are repeatedly sampled, potentially reducing model generalisation.
Undersampling majority groups may remove important examples that contain valuable information, potentially degrading overall model performance.
Does not address inherent algorithmic bias in the learning process itself, only correcting for representation imbalances in the training data.
Selection of borderline objects requires careful threshold tuning and may be sensitive to the choice of distance metrics or similarity measures used.
May not address intersectional fairness issues when multiple protected attributes create complex group combinations that require nuanced sampling strategies.

sample_claims.text: The training dataset achieves balanced representation across demographic groups without altering original qualification labels or outcome classifications
The recruitment model's training data composition is documented showing which candidate groups were preferentially sampled to address historical representation imbalances
The classification system's training data includes proportionate representation of borderline cases from all protected groups

name: Attribute Removal (Fairness Through Unawareness)
description: Attribute Removal (Fairness Through Unawareness) ensures fairness by completely excluding protected attributes such as race, gender, or age from the model's input features. While this approach prevents direct discrimination, it may not eliminate bias if other features are correlated with protected attributes (proxy discrimination). This technique represents the most basic fairness intervention but often needs to be combined with other approaches to address indirect bias through seemingly neutral features.

example_use_cases.description: Removing gender, race, and age attributes from hiring algorithms to prevent direct discrimination, whilst acknowledging that indirect bias may persist through correlated features like education institution or postal code.

Excluding protected demographic attributes from credit scoring models to comply with fair lending regulations, ensuring no explicit consideration of race, gender, or ethnicity in loan approval decisions.

Building medical diagnosis models that exclude patient race and ethnicity to prevent biased treatment recommendations, whilst ensuring clinical decisions are based solely on medical indicators and symptoms.

Creating transparent regulatory reporting systems that demonstrate compliance by explicitly documenting which protected attributes have been excluded from decision-making algorithms, providing clear audit trails for regulatory review.

limitations.description: Proxy discrimination remains a major concern as seemingly neutral features (education, postal code, previous employment) may strongly correlate with protected attributes, perpetuating indirect bias.
Intersectional bias cannot be addressed through simple attribute removal, as complex interactions between multiple demographic characteristics may create compounding discrimination effects.
Legal and regulatory compliance may be insufficient, as many jurisdictions require demonstrating disparate impact absence rather than simply removing protected attributes from models.
Identifying all potential proxy variables is practically impossible, especially with high-dimensional data where subtle correlations with protected attributes may exist in unexpected features.
Performance degradation may occur if removed attributes contain legitimate predictive information, creating tension between fairness objectives and model accuracy requirements.

sample_claims.text: The model makes decisions without direct access to protected demographic attributes such as race, gender, or age
The lending system excludes ethnicity and gender information from all decision-making processes to prevent explicit discrimination in credit approvals
The recruitment algorithm documents which protected attributes have been excluded from candidate evaluation to ensure regulatory compliance
The diagnostic system bases treatment recommendations solely on clinical indicators without incorporating patient race or ethnicity
All decision-making processes are auditable to verify that legally protected characteristics are not used as input features

name: Fair Adversarial Networks
description: Fair Adversarial Networks is a pre-processing method, proposed by Cevora (2020), that produces a de-biased copy of a dataset from which a protected characteristic such as race, sex or age can no longer be predicted, including through proxies such as postcode or occupation. It trains two neural networks against each other: an autoencoder (a network that learns to reproduce its input) rewrites each record while trying to keep it as close to the original as possible, and an adversary network tries to predict the protected characteristic from the rewritten records. The autoencoder's loss adds its reconstruction error to the adversary's predictive success, so over alternating rounds of training it learns to remove the information the adversary relies on while changing the data as little as it can. The output is the rewritten dataset, which any downstream analysis or model can use without modification, together with the evidence that a freshly trained adversary predicts the characteristic no better than always guessing the most common category.

example_use_cases.description: A probation service's analytics team wants to model reoffending from defendant records in which race is encoded indirectly, through charge descriptions and neighbourhood. It runs the records through a Fair Adversarial Network before modelling, confirms that a freshly trained classifier can no longer predict race from the transformed data better than chance, and then checks that predicted risk no longer differs by race among defendants with the same recorded outcome.

An HR analytics team at a courier company building an absenteeism model removes information about employees' age group from its personnel records, including through proxies such as length of service and family circumstances, so that the standard modelling tools its analysts already use can run on the transformed data unchanged.

A local education authority allocating support funding with a model of school performance data de-biases the data with respect to each school's majority ethnic composition before modelling, and keeps the adversary's chance-level result and the reconstruction error with the funding model's documentation as evidence of what was removed and how much the data changed.

limitations.description: No public implementation exists. The paper withholds the parts that make training practical (an approximation of how well a fully trained adversary would do, a stabilising mechanism and regularisers) as its company's intellectual property, saying only that standard approaches can replicate the result on a one-off basis with heavy tuning, and the company's web tool is no longer online. Adopting the method means reimplementing it from the paper.

It removes every trace of the protected characteristic, including relationships that are legitimate or deliberately protective; the author notes it also removes positive discrimination. Where the characteristic carries legitimate information, such as sex in some clinical data, that information goes along with the bias, and the accuracy drops seen on the demonstration datasets cannot be split into bias removed and signal lost.

Success is judged against one adversary: in the paper, a single-hidden-layer network trained from three random starts. A more capable model may still recover the characteristic from the rewritten data, and the author states that residual discrimination is likely still present and was not analysed, so a chance-level adversary is weaker evidence than it appears.

Every variable in every record can be altered by the autoencoder, so the de-biased dataset no longer contains the original values. Individual records cannot be checked against source data, feature meanings drift, and any explanation of a downstream model refers to transformed features rather than to the applicant's actual postcode or income.

Adversarial training is unstable and its settings have no principled choice: the weight balancing reconstruction against the adversary, the network architectures and the stopping point all need tuning per dataset. The paper keeps the lowest-loss state to guard against run-away training and describes its own convergence as fairly sub-optimal.

sample_claims.text: A classifier trained on the de-biased reoffending dataset cannot predict defendants' race better than always guessing the majority group.
The personnel records used to train the absenteeism model carry no recoverable information about employees' age group, including through proxies such as length of service.

The school funding model was trained on data de-biased with respect to majority ethnic composition, and its predictions no longer differ by that composition among schools with the same recorded performance.

name: Prejudice Remover Regulariser
description: An in-processing fairness technique that adds a fairness penalty to machine learning models to reduce bias against protected groups. The method works by minimising 'mutual information' - essentially reducing how much the model's predictions reveal about sensitive attributes like race or gender. By adding this penalty term to the learning objective (typically in logistic regression), the technique ensures predictions become less dependent on protected features. This addresses not only direct discrimination but also indirect bias through correlated features. Practitioners can adjust a tuning parameter to balance between maintaining accuracy and removing prejudice from the model.

example_use_cases.description: Training credit scoring models with prejudice remover regularisation to ensure loan approval decisions are not influenced by gender or ethnicity, minimising mutual information between predictions and protected attributes whilst maintaining accurate risk assessment.

limitations.description: Requires careful tuning of the fairness penalty hyperparameter, where too high values severely degrade accuracy whilst too low values provide insufficient bias mitigation.
Primarily applicable to probabilistic discriminative models like logistic regression, limiting its use with other model architectures such as deep neural networks or tree-based methods.
Computational complexity increases with the calculation of mutual information between predictions and sensitive attributes, particularly for high-dimensional data.
May not fully eliminate all forms of discrimination, particularly when complex interactions between multiple sensitive attributes create intersectional biases.
Effectiveness depends on accurate identification and inclusion of all sensitive attributes, potentially missing hidden biases from unobserved protected characteristics.

sample_claims.text: The model's loan approval predictions reveal minimal statistical information about applicants' protected demographic characteristics
The hiring system's candidate evaluations are statistically independent of gender and ethnicity identifiers

name: Meta Fair Classifier
description: An in-processing fairness technique that employs meta-learning to modify any existing classifier for optimising fairness metrics whilst maintaining predictive performance. The method learns how to adjust model parameters or decision boundaries to satisfy fairness constraints such as demographic parity or equalised odds through iterative optimisation. This approach is particularly valuable when retrofitting fairness to pre-trained models that perform well but exhibit bias, as it can incorporate fairness without requiring complete retraining from scratch.

example_use_cases.description: Retrofitting an existing hiring algorithm to achieve demographic parity across gender and ethnicity groups by using meta-learning to adjust decision boundaries, ensuring equitable candidate selection whilst maintaining the model's ability to identify qualified applicants.

limitations.description: Meta-learning approach can be complex to implement, requiring expertise in both the underlying classifier and meta-optimisation techniques.
Requires extensive hyperparameter tuning to balance fairness constraints with predictive performance, making optimisation challenging.
May result in longer training times compared to simpler fairness techniques due to the iterative meta-learning process.
Performance depends heavily on the quality and characteristics of the base classifier being modified, limiting effectiveness with poorly-performing models.
Theoretical guarantees about fairness-accuracy trade-offs may not hold in practice due to finite sample effects and optimisation challenges.

sample_claims.text: The hiring model achieves equitable selection rates across demographic groups through learned parameter adjustments that preserve candidate assessment accuracy
The fraud detection system satisfies equalised odds constraints across protected groups without requiring retraining from scratch
The environmental risk assessment model's fairness constraints are satisfied across geographic regions whilst maintaining predictive performance for resource allocation

name: Exponentiated Gradient Reduction
description: An in-processing fairness technique based on Agarwal et al.'s reductions approach that transforms fair classification into a sequence of cost-sensitive classification problems. The method uses an exponentiated gradient algorithm to iteratively reweight training data, returning a randomised classifier that achieves the lowest empirical error whilst satisfying fairness constraints. This reduction-based framework provides theoretical guarantees about both accuracy and constraint violation, making it suitable for various fairness criteria including demographic parity and equalised odds.

example_use_cases.description: Training a hiring algorithm with demographic parity constraints to ensure equal selection rates across gender groups, using iterative reweighting to balance fairness and predictive accuracy whilst maintaining legal compliance.

limitations.description: Requires convex base learners for theoretical guarantees about convergence and optimality, limiting the choice of underlying models.
Produces randomised classifiers that may give different predictions for identical inputs, which can be problematic in applications requiring consistent decisions.
Convergence can be slow and sensitive to hyperparameter choices, particularly the learning rate and tolerance settings.
Involves iterative retraining with adjusted weights, which can be computationally expensive for large datasets or complex models.
Fairness constraints may significantly reduce model accuracy, and the trade-off between fairness and performance is not always transparent to practitioners.

sample_claims.text: The lending model satisfies demographic parity constraints with quantifiable bounds on both error rate and fairness violation
The criminal justice risk assessment tool's predictions satisfy equitable treatment constraints with documented convergence properties

name: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations
description: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations (LAFTR) trains an encoder that turns each record into a representation, a vector of learned features, from which a protected attribute is hard to recover, so that models later built on that representation by other parties, including for prediction tasks not known in advance, also treat groups fairly. It was designed for a data owner who shares encoded data with downstream model builders and cannot control how they train. During training, the encoder, a decoder that reconstructs the input and a classifier for the original task play against an adversary network that tries to predict the protected attribute from the representation; the encoder is updated to defeat the adversary while keeping the information the other two need. The adversary's objective is matched to demographic parity, equalised odds or equal opportunity, and the authors prove that an optimal adversary's objective bounds that unfairness measure for any classifier trained on the representation (for the two error-rate measures the adversary also sees the labels used in training, so the attribute is hidden given the label, and the bound is with respect to those labels). The output is a frozen encoder, delivered with the accuracy and fairness of classifiers trained on top of it.

example_use_cases.description: A data marketplace that supplies customer records to advertisers wants assurance that the targeting models advertisers build will not show offers to men and women at different rates. It trains LAFTR with the demographic parity adversary, releases only the encoded features, and audits a sample of advertisers' models for the gap in positive rates and for how well a fresh classifier can recover gender from the released features.

A health insurer's data team shares encoded claims and prescription data with external analytics suppliers who build their own risk models. It trains LAFTR with an equalised-odds adversary on a comorbidity-risk task, with patients aged 70 or over as the protected group, then measures error-rate gaps for classifiers trained on held-out condition-prediction tasks, because fairness on those new tasks has to be measured rather than assumed.

A hospital imaging research group compares LAFTR with standard training for a chest X-ray triage classifier, with patient sex as the protected attribute and the model-selection rule fixed in advance, to decide whether debiasing the representation narrows the gap in error rates enough to justify its extra training cost.

limitations.description: The fairness bound holds only for an optimal adversary. A weak or under-trained adversary underestimates how much protected information the representation still carries, so downstream models can be less fair than training suggested; the authors report uneven results in places, which they attribute to unstable adversarial training. Audit downstream models directly, including with a fresh classifier trained to recover the protected attribute from the representation.

Transfer to new tasks is not guaranteed for the error-rate criteria. The equalised-odds and equal-opportunity adversaries use the original task's labels, so fairness on a new task with different labels is an empirical result: in the paper's health-data experiment LAFTR was the fairest method on seven of ten transfer tasks, and the authors leave open which tasks transfer fairly.

As formulated, it handles one binary protected attribute and a binary task label; intersectional groups, several attributes or multi-class outcomes need an extension. Training needs the protected attribute and, for the error-rate criteria, the task labels. In the paper's experiments the encoder also took the protected attribute as input, so it is needed whenever new records are encoded; no results are reported without it.

Measured gains can be small in practice. MEDFAIR, a peer-reviewed benchmark of eleven bias-mitigation methods including LAFTR on medical imaging datasets, found the methods did not significantly improve fairness over standard training when trained and tested on the same task, including across datasets (it did not test transfer to new tasks), and that the model-selection criterion changed fairness results substantially. Compare against a standard model under a selection rule stated in advance.

Up to four networks (encoder, decoder, classifier, adversary) are trained against each other, with three weights balancing accuracy, reconstruction and fairness. The paper argues reconstruction is needed for transfer and used different weights for fair classification (accuracy 1, reconstruction 0) and for transfer (accuracy 0, reconstruction 1), so settings do not carry over. The 2018 reference code pins Python 3.6 and TensorFlow 1.9; reimplementations sit inside research benchmarks.

sample_claims.text: Classifiers trained by external parties on the released representation show a demographic parity difference below the agreed threshold on every downstream task audited.

A classifier trained to recover the protected attribute from the representation released under the demographic parity objective does no better than always predicting the majority group, within an agreed margin.
The fairness of downstream risk models built on the shared encoded data was measured on each new prediction task rather than assumed from the task the encoder was trained on.
Under a model-selection rule fixed in advance, the debiased imaging model narrows the gap in error rates between patient groups relative to standard training by a measured margin.

name: Multi-Accuracy Boosting
description: An in-processing fairness technique that employs boosting algorithms to improve accuracy uniformly across demographic groups by iteratively correcting errors where the model performs poorly for certain subgroups. The method uses a multi-calibration approach that trains weak learners to focus on prediction errors for underperforming groups, ensuring that no group experiences systematically worse accuracy. This iterative boosting process continues until accuracy parity is achieved across all groups whilst maintaining overall model performance.

example_use_cases.description: Training a medical diagnosis model that achieves equal accuracy across age, gender, and ethnicity groups by using boosting to specifically target prediction errors for underrepresented patient demographics, ensuring equitable healthcare outcomes for all populations.

Building a robust fraud detection system that maintains consistent accuracy across different customer segments by iteratively correcting errors where the model performs poorly for specific demographic or geographic groups, ensuring reliable fraud prevention across all user types.

Developing a transparent hiring algorithm that provides clear evidence of equal performance across candidate demographics by using multi-accuracy boosting to systematically address group-specific prediction errors, enabling auditable fair recruitment processes.

limitations.description: Requires identifying and defining relevant subgroups or error regions, which may be challenging when group boundaries are unclear or overlapping.
Could increase model complexity significantly as the boosting process adds multiple weak learners, potentially affecting interpretability and computational efficiency.
May overfit to training data if very granular corrections are made, particularly when subgroups are small or the boosting process continues for too many iterations.
Performance depends on the quality of subgroup identification, and may fail to achieve fairness if important demographic intersections are not properly captured.
Convergence to equal accuracy across groups is not guaranteed, especially when there are fundamental differences in data distributions between groups.

sample_claims.text: The medical diagnosis system maintains equivalent prediction accuracy across patient age, gender, and ethnicity groups
The fraud detection model achieves consistent error rates across customer demographics without systematic underperformance for any group
The hiring algorithm demonstrates measurable accuracy parity across protected demographic categories with documented performance metrics for each group
The environmental risk assessment model produces equally accurate predictions across geographic regions and socioeconomic communities
The loan approval system maintains uniform prediction quality across applicant demographics without disproportionate errors for minority groups

name: Threshold Optimiser
description: Threshold Optimiser is a post-processing method, introduced by Hardt, Price and Srebro (2016), that makes an already-trained classifier's decisions meet a group fairness criterion without retraining it, most often equalised odds (equal true positive and false positive rates across groups) or equal opportunity (equal true positive rates only). Using a labelled validation set that records each person's group, it traces each group's ROC curve (the true and false positive rates obtained at every possible cut-off on the model's score) and chooses a separate cut-off for each group that maximises accuracy, or another chosen objective, subject to the criterion. When no single cut-off per group meets the criterion exactly, as is usual for equalised odds, each group's decision is randomised between two cut-offs with fixed probabilities. If the model returns only yes/no predictions rather than scores, the same method reduces to a small linear optimisation that sets, for each group and predicted label, the probability of flipping the prediction. The output is a group-aware decision rule that needs each person's group at prediction time; Fairlearn's ThresholdOptimizer implements the score-based form (and can also equalise selection rates), and AIF360's EqOddsPostprocessing implements the label-flipping form.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's model validation team applies the method to an existing credit-scoring model, choosing a separate approval cut-off for each racial group so that applicants who go on to repay are approved at the same rate in every group (equal opportunity). It compares the expected profit of that rule with a single cut-off and with an equalised-odds rule before recommending which one the credit committee should adopt.

A hospital system's data science team adjusts the alert threshold of an unplanned-readmission model separately for each race and ethnicity group, so that patients who are later readmitted are flagged at similar rates across groups. The change is accepted only because overall accuracy and daily alert volume stay within limits agreed with clinicians before the adjustment was made.

A public agency licenses a pre-trial risk tool that returns only high or low labels, with no access to scores or retraining. Using a held-out set of past cases with known outcomes, it derives the label-flipping rule that gives equal true and false positive rates across racial groups, and reports to its oversight board how many decisions the rule would change and how much accuracy it costs.

An HR analytics team piloting a CV-scoring model runs the method under equal opportunity and under equalised odds on its validation data, to show the selection panel what each criterion costs in accuracy and how many shortlisting decisions it would change. The comparison is the evidence for which fairness criterion the panel signs off before deployment.

limitations.description: The cut-off depends on the person's group, so the protected attribute must be available at the moment of decision (Fairlearn's predict requires it). Where the attribute is not collected, or where applying different cut-offs by group could count as direct discrimination or disparate treatment, which Fairlearn's own guide flags for EU and US law, the rule may be unusable in deployment even though it works in validation.

Meeting equalised odds exactly usually requires randomisation, so two people with the same score and group can receive different decisions, and Fairlearn notes that some solutions give a non-zero chance of a positive decision whatever the score. Where decisions must be reproducible or explained to the individual, such as credit refusals, this can rule the method out or force a relaxed constraint.

Under equalised odds every group's error rates are held to what the hardest-to-predict group's ROC curve allows; Hardt et al. note such a classifier must classify everyone as poorly as the hardest group. In their credit case study it kept about 80% of maximum profit against about 93% for equal opportunity, and Fairlearn warns of levelling down: worse performance for the better-served group with no gain for the worse-served one.

Cut-offs are estimated from a finite labelled sample in which group membership is known, and the original analysis sets sampling error aside. Small groups give unstable cut-offs, and rates equalised on the validation set drift when the population or the model's score distribution changes, so the cut-offs must be re-estimated and the equalised rates monitored after deployment.

Equalised odds generally conflicts with calibration within groups: Pleiss et al. (2017) show calibration is compatible with at most one equal-error-rate constraint, and Hardt et al. note that equalised odds may compromise other desirable properties of a score. A team that must show both equal error rates and calibrated risk for each group cannot obtain both from this method and may have to settle for equal opportunity alone.

sample_claims.text: The credit approval model, with per-group cut-offs set on held-out data, approves applicants who go on to repay at the same rate across racial groups, within a stated tolerance.

After group-specific threshold adjustment, the readmission alert model flags patients who are later readmitted at similar rates across race and ethnicity groups, with overall accuracy and alert volume inside the limits agreed with clinicians.
The pre-trial risk tool's post-processed decisions have equal true positive and false positive rates across racial groups on a held-out sample of past cases.
The fairness adjustment to the CV-scoring model was applied after training, leaving the trained model unchanged, and its cost in accuracy was measured and reported to the selection panel.

name: Reject Option Classification
description: A post-processing fairness technique that modifies predictions in regions of high uncertainty to favour disadvantaged groups and achieve fairness objectives. The method identifies a 'rejection region' where the model's confidence is low (typically near the decision boundary) and reassigns predictions within this region to benefit underrepresented groups. By leveraging model uncertainty, this approach can improve fairness metrics like demographic parity or equalised odds whilst minimising changes to confident predictions, thus preserving overall accuracy for cases where the model is certain.

example_use_cases.description: Adjusting hiring algorithm predictions in the uncertainty region where candidate scores are close to the threshold, reassigning borderline cases to ensure equal selection rates across gender and ethnicity groups whilst maintaining decisions for clearly qualified or unqualified candidates.

Improving reliability of loan approval systems by identifying applications where the model is uncertain and adjusting these edge cases to ensure consistent approval rates across demographic groups, reducing the risk of systematic discrimination in borderline creditworthiness assessments.

Creating transparent bail decision systems that clearly document which predictions fall within the rejection region and how adjustments are made, providing courts with explainable fairness interventions that show exactly when and why decisions were modified for equity.

limitations.description: Requires models that provide reliable uncertainty estimates or probability scores, limiting applicability to deterministic classifiers without confidence outputs.
Selection of the rejection region threshold is subjective and requires careful tuning to balance fairness improvements with accuracy preservation.
May reject too many instances if tuned conservatively, potentially affecting a large portion of predictions and reducing the model's practical utility.
Cannot address bias in confident predictions outside the rejection region, limiting effectiveness when discrimination occurs in high-certainty cases.
Performance depends on the quality of uncertainty estimates, which may be poorly calibrated in some models, leading to inappropriate rejection regions.

sample_claims.text: The hiring system's selection decisions in uncertain candidate evaluations are adjusted to ensure equal opportunity across demographic groups
The credit assessment model's predictions in borderline creditworthiness cases achieve equitable approval rates without modifying high-confidence decisions
