Where the corpus cannot be searched, the outputs are ranked by how much more probable the model finds them than a smaller reference model or a text-compression algorithm does, and the top-ranked candidates are checked by hand, for example by web search. The result is the share of generated text copied from training data (under the hand-checked route, the number confirmed among the candidates checked), the number of distinct passages extracted, and the passages themselves, each with a count of the training documents that contain it: a passage found in one or two documents is a privacy finding in a way that a licence or news story repeated thousands of times is not.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's privacy engineering team fine-tunes an open-weight language model on ten years of customer-service chat transcripts to draft replies for agents. Before deployment it generates 50 million tokens from public-text prompts with the production sampling settings, searches an index of the transcripts for 50-token matches, and looks up every account number, name and phone number tagged in the output. It runs the same test on the base model as a control.

A hospital research group that trained a clinical note-completion model on de-identified discharge summaries runs the test before sharing the weights with partner hospitals. Besides searching for verbatim passages of the summaries, it tags patient names, dates of birth and NHS numbers in the generated text and looks each up in the training set, to find identifiers the de-identification step missed and decide whether the summaries must be re-scrubbed and the model retrained.

An AI developer preparing an open-weight release compares two checkpoints, one trained on a deduplicated copy of the pre-training corpus. It generates text from each at budgets of 100 million and 1 billion tokens, counts distinct 50-token passages found verbatim in the corpus, and compares how the counts grow with the budget, not a single rate, before choosing which checkpoint to release and what to say about memorisation in the model card.

A government department running a citizen-facing chat assistant on a model it fine-tuned on casework correspondence repeats the test after every fine-tuning update. Because chat-tuned models can leak little under ordinary prompts yet emit training text once pushed off their chat behaviour, the test also uses prompts asking the assistant to repeat a single word many times, a pattern that made one production assistant reproduce its training data.

limitations.description: The result is a lower bound set by the effort spent. The number of distinct passages extracted keeps growing as more text is generated, and one study found that a model which leaked more than another at a small budget leaked less in total. A clean result, or a comparison of models at one fixed budget, can therefore mislead; report the generation budget and compare models at several budgets.

Much memorised text comes out only after the right prompt. In one study, sampling from short public prompts recovered about a third of the passages a model was known to reproduce when given their true opening words, and a chat-tuned model leaked far less under ordinary prompts than when pushed into repeating a word. A low rate under ordinary prompts is weak evidence that the data cannot be extracted.

The verdict depends on what the output is checked against and on the match rule. A public proxy for an unavailable corpus undercounts (in one study a 9 TB proxy found under half the matches a manual web search found), and a minimum match length long enough to rule out coincidence misses short secrets such as phone or account numbers unless they are tagged and looked up separately. Paraphrased leaks and facts stitched together from several documents are not counted.

It is costly at a useful scale. One study generated a billion tokens per model, and its whole evaluation, including a 45 TB index built over a 9 TB corpus, took three weeks on a large cloud machine. The test also produces copies of any personal data the model leaks, which must be stored, reviewed and deleted under the same controls as the training data.

It shows what the model emits, not what an attacker could infer. It does not say whether a known person's record was used in training, and it gives no bound for data the test did not happen to elicit, so a clean result cannot stand in for a formal guarantee such as differential privacy.

sample_claims.text: Across 50 million tokens generated from the fine-tuned support model with production sampling settings, no span of 50 or more tokens matched the training transcripts verbatim, and none of the account numbers or customer names tagged in the output occurs in the transcripts.
In an extraction test of 10 million generated tokens, the clinical note model reproduced no NHS number, and no patient name together with a date of birth, that appears in its training summaries.
At every generation budget tested, up to one billion tokens, the deduplicated checkpoint emitted fewer distinct verbatim passages of its pre-training corpus than the original checkpoint.

After each fine-tuning update, extraction tests of 20 million generated tokens, from both ordinary prompts and repeated-word prompts, found no passage of 50 or more tokens from the casework correspondence in the assistant's output.

name: Attacker-Model Re-identification Risk Measurement
description: Attacker-model re-identification risk measurement estimates, for a table of real records about people that is about to be released or shared, the probability that an attacker who links it with other information could correctly match a record to the person it describes. This record follows the attacker models of El Emam and Dankar (prosecutor and journalist) and of Dankar and El Emam (marketer), as implemented in the ARX tool: the assessor lists the quasi-identifiers (columns such as age, sex, postcode and admission date that an attacker could know or find), groups the records that share the same values on them, and names the attacker being guarded against. For a prosecutor, who knows the target is in the table, a record's risk is one over the size of its group in the table; for a journalist, who does not know this and links to a register of the wider population, it is one over the size of the matching group in that population, estimated with a statistical model when the population counts are not known; for a marketer, who tries to match as many records as possible, the measure is the expected share of records matched correctly. The assessor reports the highest record risk, the average risk and the share of records above a threshold set for the release, which decides whether the table can go out as it is or needs more generalisation or suppression first. It measures how easily records can be matched to people under the stated assumptions, unlike k-anonymity, which transforms the data, and it does not measure what can be learned about someone from values their whole group shares.

example_use_cases.description: A health insurer releasing claims data for a public prediction competition assumes an attacker who knows a neighbour's age, sex and a few of their claims, and measures each record's risk as one over the size of its group among all the insurer's members. It generalises ages and procedure codes until the measured probability of re-identification is below the 0.05 threshold agreed for the release, then checks the result with simulated matching attacks.

A pharmaceutical company sharing participant-level data from a completed trial with external researchers measures risk against the wider population, not the trial sample, because the participants are a small sample of everyone with the condition. It estimates how many records are unique in that population with ARX's uniqueness models and records the quasi-identifiers, attacker model, estimator and threshold in the data-sharing agreement for the researchers' data access committee to review.

A city transport authority planning to give a commuting dataset of home district, work district, age band and usual travel times to a contractor training a demand-forecasting model runs the assessment, finds a large share of records unique on home and work district together, merges small districts before sharing, and re-runs the assessment to confirm that the share of records above its threshold has fallen below the agreed limit.

limitations.description: The numbers are only as good as the list of quasi-identifiers and the attacker model behind them. A column left off the list, or an attacker who knows more (several of a person's hospital visits rather than one), can make records far easier to match than the assessment reports, and the assessor has to guess what other data an attacker holds. Repeating the assessment for stronger attackers, as some releases do with simulated matching, shows how sensitive the result is to these guesses.

It measures the chance of finding which record is a person's, not what can be learned about them. If all 20 records in a group share the same diagnosis, each has a measured risk of 1 in 20, yet anyone known to belong to the group has their diagnosis disclosed. Checks on the sensitive values, such as l-diversity, are needed alongside it when the release contains sensitive columns.

The journalist measure needs to know how common each record's values are in the wider population, which is rarely known and is estimated from the sample with statistical models; an evaluation of four estimators of population uniqueness on six clinical datasets found none accurate in all conditions. A small sample does not make re-identification unlikely in itself: one study estimated that 15 demographic attributes would let 99.98 per cent of Americans be correctly re-identified in any dataset.

There is no universal threshold, and the measure chosen changes the answer. For the same records the prosecutor measure is always at least as high as the journalist measure, so applying it to a release that is a small sample of a population over-protects and strips detail the data's users need; El Emam and Dankar found this effect strongest at small sampling fractions. The threshold, and which measure it applies to, must be justified for each release.

It measures one table as released, at one time. An attacker can combine several releases of the same data, or successive versions of a table that is updated, and longitudinal data, where each person has many events, need the attacker's knowledge of several events to be modelled explicitly. The basic measures do neither, so each additional or updated release needs its own assessment that takes the earlier ones into account.

sample_claims.text: Under a prosecutor attack using age band, sex and postcode district, no record in the released extract has a re-identification probability above 0.09.
The expected proportion of records in the competition dataset that an attacker could correctly match by linking it to the state voter register is below 0.1 per cent.

The re-identification risk assessment for the shared trial data states the quasi-identifiers, attacker model, population estimator and threshold used, and the highest record risk is below the agreed threshold.
Fewer than 1 per cent of records in the commuting dataset shared with the contractor are estimated to be unique in the city's population on home district, work district and age band.

name: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent
description: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) trains a neural network, or another model fitted by gradient descent, so that the finished model carries a formal differential privacy guarantee about the individual examples it was trained on. Differential privacy is more often applied by adding calibrated noise to the answer of a query or to a published statistic; DP-SGD instead changes the training algorithm itself. At each step it draws a random batch, computes the gradient (the direction in which an example pushes the model's parameters) separately for every example, scales down any gradient longer than a fixed clipping bound, adds Gaussian noise proportional to that bound to the sum, and updates the model with the noisy average, so that no single example can move the model by much and what influence remains is masked. A privacy accountant adds up the privacy cost of every step from the noise level, the sampling rate and the number of steps, and reports the total as epsilon and delta: epsilon limits how much more likely any trained model is with a given example in the training data than without it, and delta is a small probability that this limit fails. The output is a trained model with a stated (epsilon, delta) guarantee, which also covers anything later computed from the model, including its predictions.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank wants to give a credit-default model to a partner lender, which will hold the model weights. Its data science team trains the model with DP-SGD in Opacus, with each customer contributing one training example so that the guarantee protects a customer, targets epsilon 2 at a delta below one over the number of customers, and records the noise multiplier, clipping bound, sampling rate and accountant output in the model's release file.

A consortium of hospitals publishes the weights of a chest X-ray classifier so that other hospitals can fine-tune it locally. It trains with DP-SGD using one image per patient, replaces the network's batch normalisation layers with group normalisation as Opacus requires, and publishes the (epsilon, delta) guarantee and its unit, one patient, with the weights so that receiving hospitals can cite it in their own assessments.

A recruitment platform fine-tunes a language model, pretrained on public text, on job applicants' CVs (one per applicant) to suggest skills tags. It fine-tunes with DP-SGD, adds the cost of the hyperparameter search it ran on the CVs to the privacy budget, and compares tagging accuracy with a non-private fine-tune to decide whether the accuracy cost at its chosen epsilon is acceptable.

limitations.description: Clipping and noise reduce accuracy, and the reduction is not shared evenly: classes and groups that are rare in the training data lose the most, so a private model can widen an existing accuracy gap between groups. In the original experiments the drop at epsilon 8 was about 1 percentage point on handwritten digits but about 7 on a harder ten-class image task. Accuracy should be reported per group, and pretraining on public data or more training data is often needed to keep the cost acceptable.

The stated epsilon holds only if the code matches the accountant's assumptions. The usual accountants assume each batch is drawn by including every example independently at random, but many pipelines shuffle the data and cut it into fixed batches; an audit of models trained that way measured privacy loss up to four times the epsilon they reported. A claim should name the sampling method and accountant, and differential privacy auditing can test the figure empirically.

The guarantee protects one training example, not one person. If a patient has ten admissions or a customer hundreds of messages in the training set, their protection is much weaker than epsilon suggests, because the bound loosens with the number of examples they contribute. Capping each person's contribution, or making each person a single example, gives a guarantee at the level of the person, at some cost in data and accuracy.

No agreed value of epsilon makes a model private, and large values are common: the method's original headline results used epsilon 8, at which a training outcome may be about 3,000 times more likely with a given example than without it, and the Opacus image tutorial targets 50. Hyperparameter searches run on the private data also leak information unless their cost is added to the budget. A claim should state epsilon, delta, the unit of privacy and what the budget covers.

Computing a separate gradient for every example costs memory and time; in the original experiments one training epoch went from about 40 to about 180 seconds. Layers that combine examples within a batch, such as batch normalisation, break the per-example bound and must be replaced, for example with group normalisation, so an existing architecture may need changing and re-tuning before it can be trained privately.

sample_claims.text: The credit-default model shared with the partner lender was trained with DP-SGD to epsilon 2 and delta 10^-7, with each customer contributing one training example and the budget computed over every training step by the accountant in Opacus.

The published chest X-ray model weights satisfy differential privacy with epsilon 8 and delta 10^-5 with respect to any one patient, and the hyperparameter search run on patient images is included in that budget.
Training batches were drawn by Poisson sampling, matching the assumption of the privacy accountant that produced the reported epsilon.
The skills-tagging model's privacy budget of epsilon 4 per applicant covers the full fine-tuning run and every hyperparameter trial run on applicants' CVs.

name: k-Anonymity
description: k-Anonymity is a property that a table of real records about people can be made to satisfy before it is released or shared, in which every record shares its values on the quasi-identifiers with at least k-1 other records, so anyone linking the table to another source on those columns always matches a group of at least k records, which is k people only when each person has one record. Quasi-identifiers are columns that are not names or ID numbers but could be found elsewhere and combined to single a person out, such as date of birth, sex and postcode, and because the data holder chooses them, the protection covers only those columns. To reach a chosen k, each quasi-identifier is coarsened along a hierarchy set in advance (exact age to five-year band, full postcode to district), and the values or records that would still sit in a group smaller than k are suppressed, with a search choosing the coarsening that loses least information. The output is the transformed table of real records made less specific, not artificial ones, together with the k it achieves and a measure of the detail lost. Unlike differential privacy, it gives no bound on what an observer can learn, because it blocks linking on the listed columns but does not stop someone learning a sensitive value that everyone in a group shares.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital trust preparing an extract of emergency attendances for a university research team treats age, sex, postcode district and attendance date as quasi-identifiers, since local news reports and social media posts about incidents often carry them. Using ARX it generalises age to five-year bands and dates to weeks, suppresses the records still in groups smaller than five, and sends the extract with a note of the k achieved, the columns covered and the share of records suppressed.

A national statistics office preparing a scientific-use file of a household survey for registered researchers recodes region and occupation into broader groups in sdcMicro, then applies local suppression until every combination of age band, sex, region and household size occurs at least three times, and publishes the number of suppressed values with the file so that users can judge the effect on their analyses.

A motor insurer sharing a claims table with an analytics firm that will build a fraud-detection model applies 10-anonymity to policyholder age, vehicle model and postcode district. Before release it agrees with the firm that the coarser bands still carry enough signal for the model, and it keeps the generalisation scheme so that later releases are generalised from the same scheme rather than a new one.

limitations.description: k-Anonymity hides which record is a person's, not what their group has in common. If all k records in a group share the same diagnosis, anyone who can place a person in that group learns the diagnosis, and an attacker with extra background knowledge can rule out other members of the group. Extensions such as l-diversity and t-closeness add conditions on the sensitive column for this reason; k-anonymity alone does not prevent sensitive values being disclosed.

The protection covers only the columns the data holder lists as quasi-identifiers, and rests on the holder judging correctly which columns an attacker could find elsewhere. A column left off the list, such as a rare diagnosis that a local newspaper has reported, can still single a record out, and the property says nothing about it. Choosing the list needs a realistic picture of the public, commercial and leaked data an attacker could hold.

Each release is protected only on its own. Two k-anonymous versions of the same data, generalised differently or produced at different times as records are added, can be joined to narrow groups below k, and two releases that keep the rows in the same order can be lined up row by row. Later releases must be built from the first, or treat all its released columns as quasi-identifiers, and row order must be randomised before each release.

With many quasi-identifiers or detailed values such as exact dates and measurements, most records are unique, and reaching k needs coarsening or suppression heavy enough to remove the detail an analysis or model depends on; the method suits continuous variables poorly. Because the suppressed records are those with rare combinations of values, the released table can under-represent exactly the unusual cases a model most needs to handle.

Requiring k within the released table treats the attacker as knowing their target is in it. When the table is a small sample of a larger population, a record unique in the table may match many people outside it, so the requirement over-protects; El Emam and Dankar found this over-anonymisation, and the loss of information it causes, greatest at small sampling fractions. A re-identification risk assessment against the population can justify a lighter transformation.

sample_claims.text: Every record in the emergency-attendance extract shares its age band, sex, postcode district and attendance week with at least four other records.
The household survey's scientific-use file is 3-anonymous on age band, sex, region and household size, and the number of values suppressed to achieve this is published with the file.
The quasi-identifiers used for the release were chosen against a documented list of the public and commercial sources an attacker could link to, and the release is k-anonymous on all of them.
Every later release of the claims data is generalised from the same scheme as the first, as required to stop releases being joined to form groups of fewer than ten policyholders.

name: PII Detection and Redaction in Training Text
description: PII detection and redaction finds personally identifiable information (PII), such as names, email addresses, phone numbers and account or ID numbers, in a body of text and removes or replaces it before the text is used to train or fine-tune a model, so that the model has fewer personal details to memorise and later reproduce. Presidio, a widely used open-source tool first released by Microsoft and now run as an independent community project, is the reference implementation: each document passes through a set of recognisers, in which a named-entity recognition model (by default an English spaCy model) tags names, places and dates, patterns with checksum or format checks catch structured identifiers such as card and NHS numbers, and nearby words such as 'account' raise a candidate's confidence score. Every detection above a chosen score is then replaced with a placeholder for its type (for example <PERSON>), masked, hashed, encrypted or deleted, and the cleaned corpus goes to training. Because detection is never complete, the procedure ends by measuring recall, the share of identifiers actually caught, for each type on a hand-labelled sample of the same corpus. The evidence it produces is that measured miss rate and the cleaned corpus; unlike differential privacy or synthetic data, it removes real personal details from real text and gives no bound on what remains.

example_use_cases.description: A bank preparing two years of customer-service chat transcripts to fine-tune an assistant runs Presidio with added pattern recognisers for sort codes and its own account-number format, replaces each detection with a type placeholder, and has staff label 500 transcripts by hand to measure recall per entity type. It fine-tunes only once recall for names and account numbers meets the target in its data protection impact assessment, where it records the miss rate.

An NHS trust preparing discharge letters to fine-tune a summarisation model finds on a labelled sample that the default English model misses many names written in clinical shorthand and does not detect ward and bed codes at all. It adds lists of staff names and patterns for local codes, re-measures recall on a fresh labelled sample, and reports the remaining miss rate to its information governance group, which decides whether further controls are needed.

A company building a code-completion model from its internal repositories detects email addresses, IP addresses, keys and passwords with patterns and a trained detector, discards detections that are too short or are private network addresses to cut false alarms, replaces the rest with tokens such as <EMAIL> and <KEY>, and reports precision and recall per type on an annotated set of files kept apart from tuning.

limitations.description: Detection always misses some identifiers, and a model can memorise and reproduce what is missed, especially details repeated across many documents. A study that fine-tuned GPT-2 on court judgments and emails scrubbed with Presidio's default tagger and a second recogniser concluded that scrubbing reduces but cannot fully prevent leakage of personal information; Presidio's README gives no guarantee of finding it all. The evidence is a measured miss rate, not proof that none remains.

It finds only the categories it has recognisers for. On a 2022 benchmark of European Court of Human Rights judgments, Presidio's default setup caught about 70 per cent of identifying mentions but only about 45 per cent of direct identifiers, because it did not recognise case numbers, which identify the applicant on their own. Details that identify someone only in combination, such as a job title, employer and town, are not entity types at all, so redacted text can still point to a person.

The default recognisers are built for general English text. Clinical shorthand, other languages, source code and in-house identifier formats need extra recognisers or a different model, and recall measured on one corpus does not carry over to another, so the labelled sample used for the measurement must come from the corpus being cleaned and be kept apart from any tuning of the recognisers.

Raising recall by lowering the score threshold or switching on broad entity types also removes text that is not personal, such as names of public bodies, laws and places the task depends on, which lowers the value of the data for training. On the court-judgment benchmark, switching on organisation names raised Presidio's recall slightly but cut its precision from about 0.76 to 0.54.

Redaction removes identifiers from the text but does not hide whether a document was used for training, and it gives no formal bound. In the GPT-2 study, membership inference on the scrubbed model still reached an AUC of 0.82, where 0.5 is chance, and adding differentially private training brought it down to 0.5. Claims about membership, or a formal guarantee, need DP-SGD or another method alongside redaction.

sample_claims.text: Before fine-tuning, names, email addresses, phone numbers and account numbers in all customer-service transcripts were replaced with type placeholders, and recall measured on 500 hand-labelled transcripts was at least 95 per cent for each of these types.

The rate of undetected patient and clinician names left in the discharge-letter training corpus, measured on a labelled sample drawn from that corpus, is recorded in the data protection impact assessment and is below the limit set by the information governance group.

Email addresses, IP addresses, keys and passwords found in the code corpus were replaced with placeholder tokens before training, with precision and recall for each type reported on an annotated test set of files.

Recall of the redaction step is reported separately for direct identifiers and for details that identify a person only in combination, so that a high overall figure cannot hide missed direct identifiers.

name: Dangerous Capability Evaluation
description: Dangerous capability evaluation measures whether a frontier AI model can carry out tasks that could enable severe harm, such as finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, persuading or deceiving people, acquiring resources and running copies of itself, or helping to plan an attack with chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear materials, and compares the results with capability thresholds that the developer's safety framework fixes before testing. Evaluators first write a threat model for each risk domain; the framework names a critical capability level, at which the model could pose an extreme risk without extra safeguards, and an early-warning trigger defined on the evaluation results, which the method's originators sketched for one domain as success on more than half of a set of tasks given ten attempts at each. They then build task suites for each domain, such as capture-the-flag hacking challenges in sandboxed networks or multi-step tasks that require the model to set up a cloud server and install software, and try to draw out the model's best performance: it is tested without the safety filters of the deployed product, given agent scaffolding (prompts, planning loops and tools such as a command shell) and sometimes fine-tuned, because the evaluation must not underestimate what the model can do. Scoring records success over repeated attempts and, for tasks the model cannot finish, how close it came, by starting it from intermediate milestones and measuring how much expert help it needs to succeed. Unlike red teaming, which probes a system and its safeguards for whatever failures can be found, and unlike tests of whether a model refuses harmful requests, it measures what the model is able to do, and whether the results cross the trigger informs decisions on deployment and on the security measures the model needs.

example_use_cases.description: A frontier AI developer runs its cyber-offence task suite on each major checkpoint during training and before release, using the agent scaffold its evaluation team has found strongest. Its safety framework sets an early-warning trigger on the share of professional-level capture-the-flag challenges solved; a checkpoint that crosses it cannot be released until stronger protection of the model weights and mitigations against cyber misuse are in place.

A national AI security institute given access to a model before release runs autonomy tasks, such as setting up a cloud server and installing an open-source model on it, both end to end and from intermediate milestones, with a staff member approving each action the agent takes on the live internet. It reports to the developer how close the model came to completing each task and how this compares with the developer's previous model.

A company preparing to publish a model's weights openly evaluates a version fine-tuned on task-relevant data as well as the version it plans to release, because anyone who downloads the weights can fine-tune them, and compares the fine-tuned version's results with its threshold when deciding whether to publish.

limitations.description: A result below the threshold is only as strong as the effort spent drawing out the model's capability. Better scaffolds, more attempts, fine-tuning or a later checkpoint can raise scores, and models can be prompted or fine-tuned to underperform deliberately on dangerous-capability tasks while scoring normally elsewhere, so a negative result is a lower bound on capability, not proof of its absence.

The link between a task score and real-world harm is weakly grounded. The method's originators describe their early-warning trigger as early thinking in an extremely immature area and set no thresholds for their chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear evaluations, where most scientific information is dual-use, so different developers can draw the line in different places and reach different decisions from the same scores.

Task suites cover only the threat models someone has written down, and laboratory tasks may not reflect real conditions: persuasion measured in short dialogues with paid participants, or hacking measured on capture-the-flag challenges, may overstate or understate what the model could do against real people and real systems.

Agentic tasks need sandboxed environments, many repeated runs and expert grading, and tasks with real internet access need a person to approve each action so the agent cannot cause harm, which makes full runs slow and costly. Testing the unfiltered model also needs access that external evaluators may not have; testing the deployed product with its safety filters measures something different.

Results date quickly. Scores change with each new checkpoint and fine-tuning recipe, so evaluations have to be repeated for every significant model update, and published tasks can leak into training data, which is why the originating team withheld solutions and flag values from the tasks it released.

sample_claims.text: Under the strongest elicitation available to the evaluation team, the model solved fewer professional-level capture-the-flag challenges than the early-warning trigger set in the developer's safety framework.
The model did not complete any of the autonomous replication tasks end to end in ten attempts each, and needed substantial expert help to pass their intermediate milestones.
Dangerous capability evaluations were run on a fine-tuned version of the model as well as the version to be released, and neither crossed the capability threshold set before testing.
The capability thresholds and early-warning triggers used for the release decision were fixed and recorded before the evaluations were run.

name: Fault Tree Analysis
description: Fault tree analysis (FTA) is a deductive, top-down method that starts from one undesired system-level event, such as an automated braking function failing to brake for an obstacle, and works backwards to the combinations of lower-level events that could cause it. The analyst builds a tree of logic gates beneath that top event: an OR gate means any one of its inputs is enough to cause the event above it, an AND gate means all of its inputs must occur together, and the branches end in basic events such as a hardware failure, a human error or a software error. Solving the tree gives its minimal cut sets, the smallest combinations of basic events that produce the top event (a set with a single event is a single point of failure), and, when each basic event has a probability, the probability of the top event, which can be checked against a target or used to set a probability budget for each part. In a system with a machine-learning component, the model's errors enter the tree as basic events of their own, which unlike random hardware failures happen during normal operation at a rate that has to be measured on test or operational data, often depend on conditions such as weather or occlusion that can be added beneath it as conditioning events, and can be correlated from one input to the next. Working down from an acceptable top-event probability turns the model's share into a budget for its error rate, which becomes a performance requirement on the model; the tree shows where model errors matter in the system and how much error it can tolerate, but not why the model makes them.

example_use_cases.description: An avionics team designing an emergency braking system for taxiing aircraft, in which a neural network detects 'No Entry' signs, builds a quantitative fault tree for loss of the restricted-area alert, budgets the detector's misses beside the hardware failures, converts that budget into a maximum per-frame miss probability for the network, and checks on recorded taxi data whether misses in successive frames are independent, as the calculation assumes.

A driving-automation developer analysing the top event 'object not detected in time' adds weather, occlusion and lighting as triggering conditions beneath the camera detector's miss event. Quantifying the tree with rates measured on its own test drives shows which conditions dominate, and it uses the result to decide where a second sensor is needed before widening the vehicle's operating domain.

A hospital pharmacy planning to add a machine-learning dose checker beside pharmacist review draws a tree for 'harmful overdose reaches the patient', with an AND gate requiring both the checker and the pharmacist to miss the error. The analysis shows the claimed risk reduction holds only if the two misses are independent, so the team plans an audit of whether pharmacists check less carefully once the checker is live.

limitations.description: The tree explains only the top events the analysts choose and the causes they think of. Hazards nobody posed as a top event, and losses that arise from interactions between parts that each worked as specified, do not appear, so a fault tree needs a prior hazard identification to decide which top events matter.

A probability for a model-error event is only as good as the data it was measured on. A miss rate estimated on test data holds for the conditions and input mix in that data and changes when the operating environment shifts, so the top-event probability can be badly wrong in conditions the test set under-represents. The main aerospace safety-assessment guidance gives no method for such performance failures, so each assessment has to justify its own.

Quantifying a tree usually assumes basic events are independent, and machine-learning errors often are not: misses on successive camera frames are correlated, and one condition such as fog can degrade a model and the sensor or person meant to back it up at the same time. Unmodelled dependence makes an AND gate look far more protective than it is, so dependence must be checked on data or modelled explicitly.

The model appears in the tree as one or a few basic events, so the analysis says how often the model may err and where its errors matter, not why it errs or which inputs cause the errors. The triggering conditions added beneath a model-error event are only those the analysts already suspect, and finding others needs analysis of the model and its data.

Building and maintaining a tree for a large system is laborious, and it must be revised whenever the architecture or the model changes. Quantification needs a probability for every basic event, and for software, human and model events those numbers are often unavailable or disputed; aviation software guidance, for example, does not accept software reliability rates in the system safety assessment.

sample_claims.text: The quantified fault tree shows the probability of losing the restricted-area proximity alert, including the contribution of the sign detector's misses, to be below 1 in 1,000 per flight hour.

Measured on recorded taxi data, the sign detector's per-frame miss probability is below the budget derived from the fault tree, and the independence assumption used to derive that budget has been checked on the same data.
No minimal cut set for the top event 'object not detected in time' consists of the camera-based detector's miss alone.
The estimated probability of a harmful overdose reaching a patient accounts for dependence between the dose checker's misses and the pharmacist's, rather than assuming they are independent.

name: Machine Learning Failure Mode and Effects Analysis
description: Machine Learning Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (ML FMEA) applies the process form of failure mode and effects analysis, a long-established worksheet method in which a team lists what could go wrong at each step of a process, rates each failure and acts on the worst first, to the pipeline that produces a machine-learning model rather than to the model alone. The team works through the pipeline one step at a time (in the 2025 reference version: collect data requests, collect data, ingest data, validate data, preprocess data, train, tune, analyse, deploy and validate the model, and analyse feedback from the field) and, prompted by guide words such as missing, incorrect or too late, records for each step how the resulting model could fail, the effect on the wider system, the pipeline causes, and the current practices that would prevent or catch the failure. Each row is rated for severity, occurrence and detection, and the product of the three, the risk priority number, ranks the rows so that recommended actions and owners go to the highest risks first; severity is taken from the system-level hazard analysis, because the harm a model failure can do depends on the system it sits in. The method's authors publish a pre-populated template listing typical failure modes, causes and mitigations for each step, which a team tailors to its own model and application. The result is a worksheet of ranked pipeline failure modes, their controls and assigned actions, kept up to date as the pipeline changes; it looks at failures one at a time in how the model is built and does not by itself analyse how the deployed system behaves.

example_use_cases.description: An autonomous-trucking company's perception team fills in the template for its lane-detection model before each major retraining. One row under 'collect data' records that data gathered in a single season could leave the model unable to see faded or snow-covered markings; its severity comes from the vehicle-level hazard analysis, and it leads to an action, with an owner and a date, to constrain data requests by season and weather before release.

A medical-imaging company preparing a chest X-ray triage model for regulatory review uses the worksheet to show its assessors where the pipeline's controls sit. High-ranked rows include training labels taken from a single radiologist's reading, which could teach the model to miss small nodules, mitigated by double reading of a labelled sample, and online learning in deployment, mitigated by switching it off.

After a warehouse robot's object detector starts misclassifying a new kind of shrink-wrapped pallet, the vendor's safety engineer returns to the worksheet, finds that the 'analyse model feedback' step had no control for new packaging reaching customer sites, adds drift monitoring and a trigger for new data requests, and re-rates the affected rows.

limitations.description: It considers one failure mode at a time, step by step, so it does not show how failures in different steps combine, or how a model that meets its specification can still contribute to an accident through its interaction with people and other parts of the system. Teams that need those combinations and interactions have to pair it with a system-level analysis.

Severity, occurrence and detection are judgements on ordinal scales, and there is little data on how often an ML pipeline failure occurs or how reliably a control catches it. The method's authors introduced ML-specific rating criteria in 2026 because traditional FMEA criteria proved ambiguous for ML development; the public template, last updated in April 2025, has no rating criteria, so teams must set and record their own.

It analyses how the model is built, not how it behaves in use: a complete worksheet shows that known pipeline failure modes have controls, not that the deployed model performs safely. Severity has to come from a system-level hazard analysis, so the method cannot stand alone, and its authors present it as one part of a safety management system and safety case.

The pre-populated template makes a quick start but invites teams to tick through the listed failure modes instead of looking for ones specific to their system. Its examples come mostly from autonomous-vehicle development, so teams in other domains, or with other kinds of model such as language models, must add their own failure modes; the 2026 revision added steps for problem definition and for building ground truth or reward signals.

Published evidence that the method finds failures other methods miss is limited. The 2025 paper that introduced it gave no applied example, and the 2026 follow-up reporting applications to autonomous vehicles and humanoid robots is led by the method's originators: four of its twelve authors, including the first author, wrote the 2025 paper, so no independent group has yet reported using it.

sample_claims.text: Every step of the lane-detection model's development pipeline has been analysed for failure modes, and each failure mode ranked above the agreed action limit has an implemented mitigation with a named owner.
Severity ratings in the triage model's ML FMEA are taken from the system-level hazard analysis, so each pipeline risk is rated by its possible effect on patients before it is ranked.
Collection and labelling of the perception model's training data are covered by a documented control for each failure mode identified in the ML FMEA, including seasonal and weather coverage.
Following the field incident, the ML FMEA was revised to add the missing control for unseen packaging types, and the affected failure modes were re-rated.

name: System-Theoretic Process Analysis
description: System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) is a hazard analysis method developed by Nancy Leveson at MIT that treats safety as a control problem: a loss can occur when parts of a system that have not failed interact unsafely, for example when a controller acts on a wrong belief about the process it controls. The analysis has four steps: define the losses to prevent and the system-level hazards that lead to them; model the system as a control structure of controllers, the control actions they issue and the feedback they receive; identify unsafe control actions; and write loss scenarios explaining how each could arise. An unsafe control action is one of four types (not providing an action causes a hazard, providing it causes a hazard, providing it too early, too late or in the wrong order, or stopping it too soon or applying it too long), and loss scenarios cover causes such as missing or wrong feedback, a flawed control algorithm, or a controller's process model (its internal picture of what it controls) that no longer matches reality. In a system with machine-learning components, a learned model appears in the control structure as a controller whose control algorithm and process model were learned from data, or as a feedback source, such as a perception model, whose errors mislead a controller; loss scenarios include training data that missed an operating condition, a shift from training to deployment conditions, and operators who over-rely on the model, and published adaptations also model data collection, training and evaluation as control loops, so that a scenario can trace an unsafe control action back to a development decision such as an incomplete reward function. The output is a traceable set of unsafe control actions, loss scenarios and the safety constraints and requirements derived from them, which the team uses to change the design and to decide what to test; it analyses a model of the system before or alongside testing, and it gives no probabilities.

example_use_cases.description: An automotive supplier building a pedestrian collision-avoidance function around a neural-network detector models the vehicle's control structure with the detector as the braking controller's source of feedback. It finds the unsafe control action 'emergency braking not applied while a pedestrian is crossing', with scenarios such as missed detections of partly hidden pedestrians at dusk, and turns them into requirements on training-data coverage and on the detector's miss rate.

A hospital's patient-safety team preparing to deploy a machine-learning early-warning score for patient deterioration models the score, the nurses who receive its alerts and the doctors who act on them as one control structure. It finds unsafe control actions such as an escalation that comes too late because vital signs reach the record in batches, and alerts ignored after repeated false alarms, and changes data entry and the alerting rules before go-live.

A frontier AI developer's safety team analysing internal use of an AI coding agent models the engineers who prompt it, the automated monitor that scores its sessions, the human reviewers and the merge gate as controllers of the company codebase. It finds unsafe control actions such as a monitoring alert that arrives after the agent's change has been merged, and sets requirements on how quickly sessions are reviewed and on reviewers' independence from the agent.

An engineering team training a reinforcement-learning policy to land a drone splits the mission into approach, descent and touchdown, identifies unsafe control actions for each phase, such as descending too fast close to the landing pad, and uses the loss scenarios to choose the wind and sensor-noise perturbations for its simulation tests and to adjust the reward before the next round of training.

limitations.description: The analysis depends on judgement at every step: deciding which losses matter, where the system ends, which parts act as controllers and which scenarios to record. Separate teams analysing the same system can reach different models and scenario lists, so the work needs review by people outside the team, and a short list of loss scenarios is not evidence that no others exist.

STPA does not estimate how likely a hazard or scenario is, and its authors argue that such estimates are unreliable for software-intensive systems. Where an assurance case or regulator needs a quantitative target, such as a failure rate per hour, it must be paired with a quantitative method, and STPA alone cannot show that a scenario is too rare to need a mitigation.

For a learned component the analysts cannot read the process model or the control algorithm, because both are encoded in trained weights. Scenarios explaining why the model would act unsafely are therefore hypotheses about its training data and operating conditions until tests or monitoring confirm them, and for policies with continuous states and actions the analysis has to be split by mission phase or subtask to stay manageable.

A control structure that covers only the system in operation misses causes that lie in how the model was built, such as data collection, labelling, reward design or the choice of evaluation set; a survey of 31 studies applying STPA to learning-enabled systems found that most modelled operation only. Adding the development lifecycle as control loops finds these causes but makes the analysis substantially larger.

A full analysis of a complex system takes sustained effort from people trained in the method, working with domain and machine-learning experts. A language model can draft loss scenarios faster, but its drafts steer the team towards the scenarios it happens to suggest and can leave gaps, so they need the same review as scenarios written by hand.

sample_claims.text: Each unsafe control action identified for the emergency braking controller, including those caused by missed detections from the pedestrian detector, is traced to a safety constraint and to a verified requirement on the detector or the vehicle.

The hazard analysis of the early-warning score covered the clinicians who act on its alerts and the data feeds it depends on as well as the model, and every loss scenario it found has a mitigation recorded in the deployment plan.

Unsafe control actions arising from late or missing review of the coding agent's sessions were identified, and each has a design constraint that bounds the time between an agent's action and its review.
Each loss scenario derived for the drone-landing policy's approach, descent and touchdown phases is covered by at least one simulation test case.

name: Linear Bound Propagation Verification
description: Linear bound propagation verification proves that a trained neural network meets a stated property for every input in a defined region, for example that no small change to the pixels of an image alters its class, or that a controller's output stays within limits across a box of sensor readings. CROWN, the named method, replaces each neuron's activation function with two straight lines that bound it from above and below over the values that neuron can take, then works backwards from the outputs through the layers to express an upper and a lower bound on each output as a linear function of the input, and evaluates those functions over the region to obtain guaranteed numerical bounds. If the bounds show the property holds (for a classifier, that the correct class's score stays above every other class's), it is proved for the whole region; because the straight lines over-approximate the network, bounds that fail to show it leave the case undecided, so bound propagation on its own is sound but incomplete. The alpha-beta-CROWN tool tightens the bounds by tuning the lines with gradient-based optimisation and by branch and bound: for a ReLU network it splits undecided neurons into their active and inactive cases and bounds each part separately, which given enough time settles every case, making the tool complete for ReLU networks, but at a cost that can grow exponentially with the number of neurons split, so in practice each run ends as verified, falsified (a counterexample input found) or timed out. Running on graphics processors, it reaches convolutional networks with millions of parameters, larger than exact constraint solvers usually handle, at the price of leaving hard cases undecided.

example_use_cases.description: An avionics supplier's verification team checks the network that flags wildfires in airborne infrared images. For each background crop in a held-out set taken from real flight logs, it uses alpha-beta-CROWN to prove that the detector's confidence never falls as a planted fire signal grows stronger within the specified range, lists the crops where a counterexample is found, and enters the proved cases in the safety case as evidence for that consistency requirement.

A transmission system operator replaces slow time-domain simulation with a neural network that predicts whether the grid stays stable after a fault, inside the optimiser that plans generator dispatch. At each candidate dispatch its engineers use alpha-beta-CROWN to certify that the stability prediction holds for every combination of wind, solar and load within the forecast uncertainty, and raise the stability margin wherever certification fails before the plan is issued.

A pharmaceutical packaging line uses a convolutional classifier to accept or reject blister packs from camera images. Before each model release the quality team reports certified accuracy on held-out images: the share for which CROWN bounds prove that no change of up to 2/255 in any pixel can flip the decision, a bound set above the largest per-pixel noise measured on the line's cameras. A release whose certified accuracy falls well below its ordinary accuracy goes back for retraining.

limitations.description: Bound propagation on its own is incomplete: when the bounds are too loose to show the property, the case stays undecided, which is not evidence either way. Branch and bound settles more cases, but the problem is NP-complete in general, so hard cases end in a time-out. In an industrial study of an airborne wildfire detector, every query for a monotonicity property was settled, while 62 per cent of the queries for a sensor-blur property timed out.

The property must be written as a region of inputs, such as every image within a small per-pixel change of a test image or a box of sensor values, plus a linear condition on the outputs. Rotation, lighting, weather or blur are not regions of that kind; covering them means modelling them first, for example with a separate network that generates plausible blur, and the accuracy of that model then has to be argued separately.

Robustness is proved one region at a time, usually around each test input, so certified accuracy on a test set is evidence about those inputs and that perturbation only. It does not carry over to new inputs from operation, and a classifier certified around every test image can still misclassify an unperturbed image it has not seen.

It needs the whole network in a supported form (PyTorch or ONNX) and, beyond small networks, a graphics processor with enough memory: most of the tool's example configurations were tested on a 24 GB GPU, and its documented branch-and-bound support for ReLU image models reaches residual networks of about 20 layers. Layers the library does not support need their bounds written by hand, and its documented reach of millions of parameters is far below the size of large language models.

The guarantee covers the network alone. Pre-processing, sensor faults and, for a controller, the plant it drives and how errors build up over time are outside it, so a proof that a policy network never outputs an unsafe command for any state in a box does not show that the controlled system stays safe; that needs a separate analysis of the closed loop.

sample_claims.text: For every background crop in the verification set, the wildfire detection network's confidence does not decrease as fire intensity increases within the specified range.
At each dispatch issued by the preventive control planner, the stability-prediction network's output is certified unchanged for all wind, solar and load values within the forecast uncertainty set.
For at least 95 per cent of held-out inspection images, no change of up to 2/255 in any pixel can alter the classifier's accept or reject decision.
For every state in the specified operating region, the controller network's commanded torque stays within the actuator's safe limits.

name: Signal Temporal Logic Monitoring
description: Signal temporal logic (STL) monitoring checks the signals a system produces over time, such as speeds, distances, positions or a model's outputs, against safety requirements written in signal temporal logic, a formal language for stating how real-valued signals must behave over time intervals (for example, 'whenever the gap to the vehicle ahead falls below 10 m, speed drops below 5 m/s within 2 s'). Each requirement is built from comparisons of signals with thresholds, joined by logical operators and by timed operators such as 'always within [a, b]', 'eventually within [a, b]' and 'until'. For each trace the monitor computes a robustness value, a margin to the requirement rather than robustness to adversarial inputs: its sign says whether the requirement is met (positive) or violated (negative), and its size is a tolerance: any signal whose values stay closer than that to the observed ones at every instant gets the same verdict. Monitors run offline on logged or simulated traces, or online on live signals, where a requirement that looks ahead in time can be decided only once enough of the signal has arrived. RTAMT, the named tool, is an open-source Python library with an optional C++ back-end that builds such monitors from a written specification and connects to ROS and MATLAB/Simulink; its online monitors accept only requirements whose future time windows are bounded and give each verdict after a delay equal to the requirement's time horizon, and it reports the robustness value but does not act on it, so stopping or correcting the system is left to a separate safeguard.

example_use_cases.description: A team developing an adaptive cruise controller with a learned speed policy writes its requirements in STL, for example that the time gap to the vehicle ahead never stays below one second for longer than two seconds, and attaches an RTAMT monitor to every drive in an urban driving simulator. The robustness values show which controller settings meet each requirement and by what margin, and drives with negative values become regression scenarios.

A hospital's service robot, which uses learned perception to find people, fetches supplies along corridors. The integrator monitors live ROS topics against a system requirement (always at least 0.5 m from any detected person) and against one requirement per subsystem, such as the planner reaching its next waypoint in time. When a subsystem requirement fails shortly before the system one, the logged verdicts show where the fault began.

A drone-delivery operator checks each day's flight logs from its learned landing controller against a requirement that, in the last ten seconds before touchdown, descent rate stays below 1 m/s and the drone stays within 0.5 m of the pad centre. It reports the smallest robustness value across all landings to its safety manager and investigates any landing whose value is negative.

limitations.description: The monitor checks the requirement as written, not as intended. Writing correct STL needs fluency in the logic and in the system: a wrong threshold, a time window that is too short or a misplaced operator yields confident positive margins for behaviour the engineers would call unsafe, and nothing in the monitor reveals the mistake. Specifications need the same review as the requirements they encode.

Online monitoring judges a requirement from a partial trace. RTAMT's online monitors take only requirements whose future time windows are bounded, and give each verdict after a delay equal to the requirement's horizon: a check that something happens within five seconds is decided five seconds later, which may be too late to act on in a fast system. Monitors that track a narrowing range of possible robustness values can flag some violations sooner, but stay undecided until the data settles it.

A robustness value is measured in the units of the signals in the requirement, so a margin of 0.4 means 0.4 metres in one requirement and 0.4 degrees in another. Values cannot be compared across requirements, and when one requirement combines signals of different scales its value is set by whichever margin is numerically smallest, which depends on the units chosen unless the signals are normalised first.

Monitoring reports on the traces it sees. A clean record over many hours shows that those runs met the requirement, not that every possible run will, and a violation is reported when it happens, not before, unless a separate predictor of future signals is added. To protect the system, the verdict has to drive a safeguard such as a fallback controller, which the monitor does not provide.

The verdict is only as good as the signals. If a learned perception component misjudges the distance to a person, the monitor computes a confident margin from the wrong distance; independent sensors or ground truth are needed to check the perception itself. Discrete-time monitors see only the samples taken, so a brief violation between samples can go unseen, and the ROS integration assumes messages arrive at a known, regular rate.

sample_claims.text: In every simulated and test-track drive of the release campaign, the adaptive cruise controller met the minimum time-gap requirement, and the smallest robustness margin is reported for each scenario.
Throughout the trial period the service robot's online monitor recorded no violation of the 0.5 m separation requirement, and each subsystem-level violation it logged was investigated and closed.
Every landing made by the learned landing controller in the reporting period met the final-approach descent-rate and position requirements, with the smallest margin stated.

name: SMT-Based Neural Network Verification
description: SMT-based neural network verification decides exactly whether any input in a defined region can make a trained neural network violate a stated property, and if one can, returns that input as a counterexample. SMT (satisfiability modulo theories) solvers decide whether a set of logical and arithmetic constraints can all hold at once: here the network's weighted sums become linear equations, each piecewise-linear activation such as ReLU becomes a constraint with two cases (inactive at zero, or active and passing its input through), and the input region and the negation of the property become further linear constraints. The solver searches for values that satisfy every constraint with a simplex-based linear-programming engine: it first tries to repair an activation whose current values break it, and splits it into its two cases only when repairs keep failing, while bounds on each neuron (in Marabou, by default, the linear bounds that bound propagation computes) rule cases out early. Reluplex (Katz et al., 2017) introduced this lazy treatment of ReLU inside the simplex method and used it on a prototype airborne collision avoidance network; Marabou, its maintained successor, keeps the same search structure with a newer search procedure, adds parallel solving, and can emit a proof certificate for an 'unsatisfiable' answer. The answer is 'unsat', meaning no input in the region violates the property, or 'sat' with a concrete counterexample, and for networks whose activations are all piecewise-linear the procedure is complete; the price is that the number of cases can grow exponentially with the number of neurons, so it is practical for small networks such as controllers, policies and surrogate models with few inputs rather than large image models.

example_use_cases.description: A warehouse robotics team trains hundreds of candidate deep reinforcement learning policies for driving between shelves from range-sensor readings. Before field trials it encodes 'no move into an obstacle in the next step' and 'no repeating left-right loop over several steps' as queries over each small policy network, runs Marabou on every candidate, discards each policy for which a counterexample reading is returned, and takes only the survivors to the physical robot.

An aircraft systems developer replaces a large collision-avoidance lookup table with a set of small neural networks. For each network it writes regions of encounter geometry, such as an intruder close ahead and closing, together with the advisory that must never be issued there, and runs the solver on each. Regions returned as unsatisfiable go into the certification evidence; any counterexample encounter is replayed in simulation and drives retraining.

A medical-device manufacturer uses a small network to recommend infusion rates from a handful of patient measurements. Its safety engineers prove that, for every combination of measurements within the clinically plausible ranges, the recommended rate never exceeds the maximum set by the device's hazard analysis, and use any counterexample returned to retrain the network or add an output limit.

limitations.description: Deciding these queries for ReLU networks is NP-complete, and the search may split on every neuron whose case is undecided, so time can grow exponentially with network size and with the number of steps a property spans. In a study of robot navigation policies kept to 16 neurons per hidden layer, single-step collision queries took seconds, but 12-step cycle queries usually ran for hours and nearly three in ten of them hit the 12-hour limit.

The solver runs on ordinary processors, and its own tool paper reports a non-trivial performance gap to GPU-based bound-propagation verifiers, especially on larger networks; in the 2023 verification competition it solved 594 benchmark instances to alpha-beta-CROWN's 721. It is therefore best suited to small networks with few inputs, such as controllers, policies and surrogate models.

Exact answers hold only for piecewise-linear activations such as ReLU, max, absolute value and leaky ReLU. Sigmoid and tanh are handled by an over-approximation that is refined step by step, and softmax and bilinear layers only through a convex relaxation, so for networks that use them the procedure is no longer complete and can end without a decisive answer.

The query covers the network and a region of its inputs written as linear constraints, nothing more. A counterexample may lie in a part of the region no real sensor could produce, and a proof says nothing about the environment the network acts in, so choosing a region that is realistic yet small enough to solve takes domain knowledge, and a closed-loop safety claim needs further analysis.

An 'unsat' answer is only as trustworthy as the solver's implementation. Marabou can emit a proof certificate that an independent checker validates, but proof production works with only some of its features and not in parallel mode, and in the tool paper's collision-avoidance experiments certificates were produced for 113 of 180 benchmarks.

sample_claims.text: None of the navigation policies released for field trials can command a move into an obstacle within one step from any range-sensor reading in the specified input region.
For every encounter geometry in each specified region, the collision-avoidance network never issues a 'clear of conflict' advisory while the intruder is inside the protected volume.
For all patient measurements within the clinically plausible ranges, the infusion network never recommends a rate above the maximum set by the hazard analysis.
Every counterexample returned while verifying the candidate controllers was replayed in simulation, and every released controller was re-verified and found to have none.

name: Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law Risk and Impact Assessment
description: HUDERIA is the Council of Europe's methodology for identifying and assessing the risks an AI system poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law, and for planning how to prevent or reduce them, from design through deployment to retirement. It is non-binding guidance that public and private organisations may use or adapt in whole or in part; it was drawn up to support risk assessment in line with the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, and the human rights treaties its resources cite are illustrative, binding only the states that are parties to them. A multidisciplinary team first runs a context-based risk analysis (COBRA): it scopes the system's purpose, data and affected groups, works through risk factors in the system's application, design and deployment contexts, maps potential impacts on specific rights and on democratic and legal processes, gives each impact an initial rating, and triages the system, deciding whether further assessment is needed and whether the system should be built or deployed at all. Impacts are rated for severity, judged by scale (how serious the harm is), scope (how many people, which groups and for how long) and reversibility (whether those affected can be restored to their earlier position), and for probability; for systems that may pose significant risks, the team may engage affected stakeholders and then re-examines and re-rates each impact in a fuller risk and impact assessment. The output is a mitigation plan that prefers avoiding a harm to reducing, repairing or compensating for it, names who is responsible for each measure, outlines where appropriate the remedies open to affected people, and schedules repeat reviews as the system and its context change.

example_use_cases.description: A city council's children's services department is offered a model that ranks safeguarding referrals for follow-up. A team of caseworkers, a data scientist and a human rights lawyer runs the context-based risk analysis, maps impacts on family life, non-discrimination and fair procedure, and at triage asks whether existing caseworker screening would serve the problem better and whether the referral data represent the families concerned, before deciding whether to procure the model at all.

A recruitment software company assessing a CV-screening model engages disabled and older job seekers, the groups its analysis found most exposed, then rates each mapped impact for scale, scope, reversibility and probability under a scoring rule it writes down. Its mitigation plan drops a feature that scored video interviews, an 'avoid' measure, rather than relying on correcting decisions afterwards, and names the owner of each remaining measure.

A national tax authority that assessed its fraud-risk model before launch repeats the risk and impact assessment when it adds bank-transaction data, and again when a change in benefit rules alters who is flagged. Each review updates the mitigation plan and the information and appeal routes offered to people wrongly flagged, so the assessment on file describes the system as it now runs.

A health ministry outside Europe adapts HUDERIA for a symptom-checker chatbot, keeping the treaty references in the risk-factor and impact lists only for the instruments its state is party to and adding its own constitution, health law and data protection law, while keeping the four elements and the severity variables so that its assessments follow a published structure others can recognise and check.

limitations.description: HUDERIA leaves the rule for combining scale, scope, reversibility and probability into a risk level, and the thresholds used at triage, to the authorities or project teams applying it. Two teams can rate the same system differently and both be following the methodology, so an assessment can be compared or checked only if the team records the scoring rule it chose and why.

Stakeholder engagement and the detailed risk and impact assessment are optional, and are expected mainly for systems that the team's own triage finds may pose significant risks. A team that under-rates a system at triage can skip the stages most likely to expose the problem, so the evidence is stronger when someone outside the team has reviewed the triage reasoning.

The assessment rests on documents, expert judgement and what stakeholders report; it does not test the system. Probability ratings made before a system is built can be little more than informed estimates, so claims about how the system actually behaves, for example whether it treats groups differently, need test results from other techniques alongside the assessment.

HUDERIA assesses one system at a time. It asks teams to consider cumulative effects when a system runs alongside others serving similar purposes, which is where many harms to democratic and legal processes arise, but gives no method for estimating them. An assessment can therefore find each system acceptable while their combined contribution to a wider harm goes unmeasured, so claims about societal impact need evidence beyond a single assessment.

A full assessment needs people who can judge impacts on rights in law as well as people who understand the system's data and design, and it is meant to be repeated over the system's life. Organisations without access to human rights legal expertise may be unable to carry out the impact mapping and mitigation planning to the depth the methodology intends.

sample_claims.text: Before procurement, the safeguarding referral model went through a documented HUDERIA context-based risk analysis, and the triage decision, including whether to adopt the system at all, is recorded with its reasons.

Every impact identified for the CV-screening model was rated for scale, scope, reversibility and probability under a written scoring rule, and each impact rated high has a mitigation measure with a named owner.
Groups identified as most exposed to the system's potential harms were consulted before the risk and impact assessment, and the assessment records which impacts their input added or changed.

The risk and impact assessment of the fraud-risk model has been repeated after each change to its data sources or to the rules it applies, and the mitigation plan and the remedies for people wrongly flagged were updated each time.

name: AI Incident Reporting with the OECD Common Reporting Framework
description: AI incident reporting with the OECD common reporting framework records each event in which an AI system caused harm, or could plausibly have caused it, in the common set of 29 fields the OECD published in February 2025, so that reports from different organisations, sectors and countries can be compared and pooled. The framework is meant for both mandatory and voluntary reporting and defines what a report contains, not the reporting interface or what should happen afterwards. The reporter first classifies the event using the OECD's definitions: an AI incident is an event in which the development, use or malfunction of an AI system directly or indirectly leads to harm to people's health, disruption of critical infrastructure, a violation of human rights or of laws protecting fundamental, labour or intellectual property rights, or harm to property, communities or the environment, and an AI hazard is one that could plausibly lead to such harm. Seven fields are mandatory: a title, a description, how the AI system was involved (as a direct cause, a contributing factor, a failure to act, through over-reliance or misuse, through human error, or through a failure to comply with the law), who is reporting, supporting material, the severity (hazard, serious hazard, incident, serious incident or disaster) and the type of harm. The other 22 record, where known and among other things, when and where it happened, the system and the organisations behind it, the people affected, the sector, how widely the system was deployed, whether training data, the model or several interacting systems were involved, the system's task and level of autonomy, and any action taken, giving an inspectable register of what went wrong in operation.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's model risk team logs every complaint from customers or staff about its credit, fraud and customer-chatbot models that meets the OECD definition of an AI incident or hazard. A wrongly refused loan, an account frozen by a fraud alert and a chatbot quoting the wrong fees are recorded on the same severity scale and harm types, with the model and version and how the model was involved, so the quarterly risk committee can see which systems recur and which harms dominate.

A hospital records near misses as well as harms. When a radiologist notices that the imaging triage model has put an urgent scan at the back of the queue, the event is logged as an AI hazard, with the model's erroneous ranking as a direct cause, its autonomy recorded as human-in-the-loop, and the action taken, so that patterns of near misses are visible before one becomes an incident.

A national regulator that receives AI incident reports from deployers in several sectors asks for them in the OECD format, with a published note on how it judges seriousness, so that it can count serious incidents by sector and harm type and compare its figures with those of other authorities using the same fields.
